rev.x: Investment in real estate offers advantages of

i: leverage, which is offered by the use of borrowed money;
above-average rate of return, generally;
greater control than ownership of securities;
tax benefits in certain situations;
income (cash flow) production; and
possibility of property appreciation (increase in value over time).

rev.x: Disadvantages of investment in real estate include

i: lack of liquidity (ready conversion into cash),
high cost to acquire,
active management or cost of hiring a professional property manager, and
high degree of risk, although an investor's ability to hold onto property long term tends to reduce risk.

rev.x: Cash flow of income property, the amount remaining after all ownership expenses have been paid, tends to make it the safest form of real estate investment, but note the following:

i: Rent paid by tenants is a major source of property income and depends on the property's location, physical appearance, and available amenities.
When rent does not cover property expenses, negative cash flow results.

rev.x: Pyramiding is a method of using the ownership of one property to drive the acquisition of more properties and usually consists of the following types:

i: In pyramiding through selling, the investor acquires a property, improves it for resale at a substantially higher price, and then uses the profit from the sale to purchase another property.
In pyramiding through refinance, the investor uses the refinance proceeds of one property to purchase new properties.

rev.x: The tax benefits of owning investment real estate depend on current tax law.

i: Capital gain is the difference between the adjusted cost basis of a property and its net selling price, and it may be taxed at a more favorable rate than a taxpayer's earned income.
Adjusted cost basis is the investor's acquisition cost, plus the cost of any physical improvements made to the property, and less the amount of any depreciation claimed as a tax deduction.
Depreciation (cost recovery) allows an investor to recover the cost of an income-producing asset through tax deductions over the asset's useful life:

Straight-line depreciation divides the cost attributable to the building by the number of years of projected useful life, currently set by federal law at 27.5 years for residential real estate and 39 years for commercial real estate.

Accelerated cost recovery system (ACRS) allows taxpayers to claim greater deductions in the early years of ownership, reducing the amount that may be deducted in each subsequent year of a property's defined useful life.
Losses from the sale of a real estate investment may be deductible.
Tax credits (direct reductions of tax owed) are available for the renovation of older buildings, low-income housing projects, and historic properties.

rev.x: Exchanges offer investors the opportunity to defer the payment of taxes on profit indefinitely:

i: Property may be exchanged for other like-kind property.
Property owner is taxed only on additional capital or property received as part of the exchange (boot).
Tax is deferred (not eliminated), with the capital gain taxed on the eventual sale.

rev.x: A real estate investment syndicate is a business venture in which participants pool resources to own or develop property. Pooling of funds may involve securities registration under federal and state securities laws.

A real estate investment trust (REIT) does not pay corporate income tax as long as 95 percent of its income is distributed to its shareholders and other conditions are met. Restrictions and regulations on the formation and operation of REITs are complex.
A real estate mortgage investment conduit (REMIC) has complex qualification, transfer, and liquidation rules; it is notable because of the asset test requirement.

b.x: Real estate is a popular investment. Whichever way the overall market turns, the real estate investment market continues to initiate innovative and attractive investment strategies. These developments make it important for real estate licensees to have an elementary and up-to-date knowledge of real estate investment. Most homebuyers will also want assurance that a residential purchase is a good investment. A licensee should never act as an investment advisor but should instead refer investors to competent tax accountants, attorneys, or investment specialists.

In recent years, real estate values nationwide have significantly changed. Some investments have failed to produce returns greater than the rate of inflation, but some real estate investments have shown above-average (or even high) rates of return. In theory, this means that an investor can use borrowed money to finance a real estate purchase and feel relatively sure that an asset, if held long enough, will return more money than the cost to finance the purchase.
Real estate offers investors a greater control over their investments than other options, such as stocks, bonds, or other securities. Real estate investors also receive certain tax benefits.

Disadvantages of Real Estate Investment (1 of 2) Unlike stocks and bonds, real estate is not highly liquid over the short term. Liquidity refers to how quickly an asset may be converted into cash. For instance, an investor who holds stocks can easily direct a stockbroker to sell stocks when funds are needed. The stockbroker sells the stock and the investor receives the cash. In contrast, a real estate investor may have to sell the property at a substantially lower price than desired to ensure a quick sale or to refinance the property.

Real estate investments are expensive. Large amounts of capital are usually required. Investing in real estate is difficult without expert advice. Investment decisions must be based on careful studies of all the facts, reinforced by a thorough knowledge of real estate and how it is affected by the marketplace.

Disadvantages of Real Estate Investment (2 of 2) Real estate requires active management. A real estate investor can rarely just sit and watch the money grow. Management decisions must be made. How much rent should be charged? How should repairs and tenant grievances be handled? The investor may choose to personally manage the property or hire a professional property manager.

Finally, despite its popularity, real estate investment does not guarantee profit. It involves a high degree of risk. The possibility that an investment property will decrease in value or not generate enough income to make it profitable is a fluctuating factor for the investor to consider.
The advantages and disadvantages of real estate investments are listed in the table below.

Real estate investors anticipate various investment objectives. Their goals can be reached more effectively depending on the type of property and ownership they choose. The most prevalent form of real estate investment is direct ownership. Both individuals and corporations may own real estate directly and manage it for appreciation or cash flow (income). This type of real estate is known as income property.
Real estate is an avenue of investment open to those interested in holding property primarily for increasing value, which is known as appreciation.

Two main factors affect appreciation: inflation and intrinsic value. Inflation is the increase in the amount of money in circulation. When more money is available, its value declines. When the value of money declines, wholesale and retail prices rise. This is essentially an operation of supply and demand, as discussed in Unit 1. An intrinsic valueof real estate is the result of a person's individual choices and preferences for a given geographic area. For example, property located in a pleasant neighborhood near attractive business and shopping areas has a greater intrinsic value to most people than similar property in a more isolated location. As a rule, the greater the intrinsic value, the more money a property commands on its sale.

Often, investors speculate in purchases of either agricultural land or undeveloped land located in what they expect to be a major path of growth. In these cases, however, the property's intrinsic value and potential for appreciation are not easy to determine. This type of investment carries many inherent risks. How fast will the area develop? Will it grow sufficiently for the investor to make a good profit? Will the expected growth occur? More important, will the profits eventually realized from the property be great enough to offset the costs of holding it, such as
property taxes? Because these questions often cannot be answered with any degree of certainty, lending institutions may be reluctant to lend money for the purchase of raw land.

Income tax laws do not allow for the depreciation of land. Land also might not be liquid (salable) at certain times under certain circumstances because few people will purchase raw or agricultural land on short notice. Despite all the risks, land has historically been a good inflation hedge if it is held for the long term.
Investment in land ultimately is best left to experts, and even they frequently make bad land investment decisions.
A person who wishes to buy and personally manage real estate may find that rental income property is the best investment.
Cash Flow

The objective of directing funds into income property is to generate spendable income, called cash flow. Cash flow is the total amount of money remaining after all expenditures have been paid. These expenses include taxes, operating costs, and maintenance. The cash flow produced by any given parcel of real estate is determined by at least three factors: amount of rent received, operating expenses, and method of debt repayment.

Generally, the amount of rent (income) that a property commands depends on a number of factors, including the property's location, physical appearance, and amenities. If the cash flow from rents is not enough to cover all expenses, negative cash flow may result. For example, the table below shows a negative cash flow.
To keep cash flow high, an investor should attempt to keep operating expenses reasonably low. Such operating expenses include general building maintenance, repairs, utilities, and tenant services.

An investor often stands to make more money by investing with borrowed money, usually obtained through a mortgage loan or deed of trust loan. Low mortgage payments spread over a long period result in a higher cash flow because they allow the investor to retain more income each month. In turn, high mortgage payments contribute to a lower cash flow.
The chart below shows the cash flow on a partially tax-sheltered property.

Income-producing properties include apartment and office buildings, hotels, motels, shopping centers, and industrial properties, but some communities have experienced severe overbuilding of office space and shopping centers. The result has been higher-than-average vacancy rates.

Leverage is the use of borrowed money to finance an investment. As a rule, an investor can receive a maximum return from the initial investment by making a small down payment, paying a low interest rate, and spreading mortgage payments over as long a period as possible.

The effect of leveraging is to provide a return that reflects the result of market forces on the entire original purchase price but that is measured only against the actual cash invested. For example, if an investor spends $100,000 for rental property, makes a $20,000 down payment, and then sells the property five years later for $125,000, the return over five years is $25,000.
Disregarding ownership expenses, the return is not 25 percent ($25,000 compared with $100,000), but 125 percent of the original amount invested ($25,000 compared with $20,000).

Risks are directly proportionate to leverage. A high degree of leverage translates into greater risk for the investor and the lender because of the high ratio of borrowed money to the value of the real estate. Lower leverage results in less risk. When property values drop in an area or vacancy rates rise, the highly leveraged investor may be unable to pay even the financing costs of the property.

Equity buildup is a result of a loan payment directed toward the principal rather than the interest, plus any gain in property value due to appreciation. In a sense, equity buildup is like money in the investor's bank account. This accumulated equity is not realized as cash unless the property is sold, refinanced, or exchanged.

An effective method for real estate investors to increase their holdings without investing additional capital is through pyramiding. Pyramiding is the process of using one property to drive the acquisition of additional properties. Two methods of pyramiding can be used: pyramiding through sale and pyramiding through refinance.

In pyramiding through sale, an investor first acquires a property and then improves it for resale at a substantially higher price. The profit from the sale of the first property is used to purchase additional properties. The disadvantage is that the proceeds from each sale are subject to capital gains taxation.

FOR EXAMPLE A woman bought a house for $340,000. She put an addition on the house and a new roof. In three years, the woman sold the home for $420,000. After deducting commission and selling expenses, she used the $80,000 profit to buy another property.

The goal of pyramiding through refinancing is to use the value of the original property to drive the acquisition of additional properties while retaining all the properties acquired. The investor refinances the original property and uses the proceeds of the refinance to purchase additional properties. These properties are refinanced, enabling the investor to acquire further properties. By holding on to the properties, the investor may delay the capital gains taxes that would result from a sale.

Income tax laws change frequently, and some tax advantages of owning investment real estate are altered periodically by Congress. An investor can make a more educated and profitable real estate purchase with professional tax advice.

Capital gain is defined as the difference between the adjusted basis of property and its net selling price. At various times, the tax law has excluded a portion of capital gains from income tax and taxed various types of gains differently.
Basis

A property's cost basis determines the amount of gain to be taxed. The basis of the property is the investor's initial cost of the real estate. The investor adds to the basis the cost of any physical improvements subsequently made to the property. The amount of any depreciation claimed as a tax deduction is subtracted from the basis. The result is the property's adjusted
basis. When the investor sells the property, the amount by which the sales price exceeds the property's adjusted basis is the capital gain.

FOR EXAMPLE Some time ago, an investor purchased a single-family home for use as a rental property. The purchase price was $95,000. The investor now sells the property for $200,000. Shortly before the sale date, the investor makes $5,000 worth of capital improvements to the home. Depreciation of $15,000 on the property improvements has been taken during the term of the investor's ownership.
The investor will pay a broker's commission of 7 percent of the sales price. The investor's closing costs will be $800. The capital gain is computed as follows:

Depreciation, or cost recovery, allows an investor to recover the cost of an income-producing asset through tax deductions over the asset's useful life. Though investors rarely purchase property without expecting it to appreciate over time, the tax laws maintain that all physical structures deteriorate (and lose value) over time. Cost recovery deductions may be taken only on personal property and improvements to land.

Depreciation taken periodically in equal amounts over an asset's useful life is called straight-line depreciation. For certain property purchased before 1987, it was also possible to use an accelerated cost recovery system (ACRS) to claim greater deductions in the early years of ownership, gradually reducing the amount deducted in each year of useful life. The Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997 established specific rules governing holding periods and taxability of depreciation for real property. Depreciation is set by statute. Currently, statutory depreciation is 27.5 years for residential real estate and 39 years for commercial real estate.

Real estate investors can defer taxation of capital gains by making property exchanges. Even property that has appreciated greatly since its initial purchase may be exchanged for other property. A property owner will incur tax liability on a sale only if additional capital or property is also received: the tax is deferred, not eliminated. Whenever the investor sells the property, the capital gain will be taxed. In many states, state income taxes can also be deferred by using the exchange form of property transfer.

To qualify as a tax-deferred exchange, the properties involved must be of like kind as defined under Section 1031 of the Internal Revenue Code. The exchanged property must be real estate of equal value and same use. Any additional capital or personal property included with the transaction to even out the value of the exchange is called boot. The IRS requires tax on the

boot to be paid at the time of the exchange by the party who receives it. The value of the boot is added to the basis of the property for which it is given. Tax-deferred exchanges are governed by strict federal requirements, and competent guidance from a tax professional is essential.

FOR EXAMPLE A person owns an apartment building with an adjusted basis of $225,000 and a market value of $375,000. That person exchanges the building plus $75,000 in cash for another apartment building having a market value of $450,000. That building has an adjusted basis of $175,000. The owner's basis in the new building is $300,000 (the $225,000 basis of the building exchanged plus the $75,000 cash boot paid), and there is no tax liability on the exchange. The previous owner of the new building must pay tax on the $75,000 boot received and has a basis of $175,000 (the same as the previous building) in the building now owned.

In addition to tax deductions for depreciation, investors may be able to deduct losses from their real estate investments. The tax laws are very complex. The amount of loss that may be deducted depends on whether an investor actively participates in the day-to-day management of the rental property or makes management decisions. Other factors are the amount of the loss and the source of the income from which the loss is to be deducted. Investors who do not actively participate in the management or operation of the real estate are considered passive investors. Passive investors may not use losses to offset active income derived from active participation in real estate management, wages, or income from stocks, bonds, and the like. The tax code cites specific rules for active and passive income and losses and may be subject to changes.
Certain tax credits are allowed for the renovation of older buildings, low-income housing projects, and historic property. A tax credit is a direct reduction in the tax due rather than a
deduction from income before tax is computed. Tax credits encourage the revitalization of older properties and the creation of low-income housing.
A taxpayer who sells real property and receives payment on an installment basis pays tax only on the profit portion of each payment received. Interest received is taxable as ordinary income.

A real estate investment syndicate is a business venture in which people pool their resources to own or develop a particular piece of property. This structure permits people with only modest capital to invest in large-scale operations. Typical syndicate projects include highrise apartment buildings and shopping centers. Syndicate members realize some profit from rents collected on the investment. The main return usually comes when the syndicate sells the property.

Syndicate participation can take many legal forms. For instance, syndicate members may hold property as tenants in common or as joint tenants. Various kinds of partnership, corporate, and trust ownership options are possible.

Private syndication generally involves a small group of closely associated or experienced investors. Public syndication involves a much larger group of investors who may or may not be knowledgeable about real estate as an investment. Any pooling of individuals' funds raises questions of securities registration under federal and state securities laws, known as blue-sky laws.

By directing their funds into a real estate investment trust (REIT), real estate investors take advantage of the same tax benefits as do mutual fund investors. A real estate investment trust does not have to pay corporate income tax as long as 95 percent of its income is distributed to its shareholders. Certain other conditions also must be met. To qualify as a REIT, at least 75 percent of the trust's income must come from real estate. Investors purchase certificates in the trust, which in turn invests in real estate or mortgages (or both). Profits are distributed to investors.

A real estate mortgage investment conduit (REMIC) has complex qualification, transfer, and liquidation rules. For instance, the REMIC must satisfy the asset test. The asset test requires that after a start-up period, almost all assets must be qualified mortgages and permitted investments. Furthermore, investors' interests may consist of only one or more classes of regular interests and a single class of residual interests. Holders of regular interests receive interest or similar payments based on either a fixed rate or a variable rate. Holders of residual interests receive distributions (if any) on a pro rata basis.

t: Iowa Real Estate Commission and Licensing

i: The IREC is made up of seven members, each residing in a different Iowa county.

rev.x: Five are Iowa real estate licensed members (one must be a licensed salesperson) and two are nonlicensees.

i: Licensed members of the IREC are required to have at least five years of real estate experience.
IREC members are not allowed to hold any elective or appointive state or federal office simultaneously with their term.
IREC appointments are for three years. No member is allowed to serve more than three consecutive terms, or nine years, total.
The mission of the IREC is to protect the public through the examination, licensing, and regulation of real estate brokers, salespersons, and firms.

A real estate license is required for those who, with the intent of compensation, perform the services of a licensee, whether as a part of a transaction or as an entire transaction, or represent themselves as licensees.
The most important exception to the licensing requirement is those persons who act on their own behalf. Any persons can list, buy, rent, or sell their own property.
Iowa recognizes licensure in other states with reciprocity agreements.

A partnership, association, or corporation is not granted a license unless every member and/or employee who actively participates in the brokerage business holds a real estate license and at least one officer, partner, or member has to hold a broker's license. Basic license requirements include minimum age of 18 years, prelicensing education and testing, and a national criminal history check through the FBI.
The Commission may deny a license for several reasons under the Iowa Code, Section 543B.15.
There is only one designated broker in an office or branch office. The other people in the office may hold salesperson's or broker's licenses.

An applicant for the salesperson licensing exam must successfully complete a Commission-approved course in real estate principles and practices of at least 60 classroom or computer-based hours. The applicant must complete a total of 96 hours of the required education during the 12 months prior to date of licensure application.

The broker candidate must be actively licensed as a salesperson for at least 24 months. Qualified applicants for a broker's license must complete a Commission-approved course of at least 72 classroom hours.
All licenses (including inactive licenses) are issued for three-year terms and expire on December 31 of the third year of licensure.
Licensees must complete 36 approved continuing education hours during their licensing term with at least 12 hours of continuing education taken in the classroom.
The immediate license transfer process involves three steps.
With proper disclosure it is legal for a licensee to buy and/or sell property for his or her own benefit.
Licensees may sell or buy property for themselves with or without going through their broker.
Licensees who engage personal assistants have the primary responsibility for their supervision.
Under direct supervision of a licensee, Iowa law permits unlicensed assistants to perform certain tasks.
The selling of chances (lotteries) by a real estate brokerage firm is illegal in Iowa.

b.x: Real estate practices in Iowa are governed by the Code of Iowa, Chapters 543B and 558A, "Real Estate Brokers and Salespersons and Real Estate Disclosures." See the Law Index on the Iowa Professional Licensing Bureau Web site. This law also authorizes the Iowa Real Estate Commission (IREC) to adopt a set of administrative rules and regulations to define the statutory law. Iowa Real Estate Commission Administrative Rules 193E have the same force and effect as the law and provide more detail for the administration of the law as well as guidelines for the real estate licensee. See the Administrative Rules on the Iowa Professional Licensing Bureau Web site for more information.
The IREC annually publishes changes to the code and the rules online. See the Rule Changes on the Iowa Professional Licensing Bureau Web site.
This unit covers the Real Estate Licensing Commission and licensing issues: activities requiring licensure and exemptions, license categories, and licensing requirements and renewals.

Instead of having a Commissioner to regulate real estate activity, Iowa has a seven-member body that makes up the Iowa Real Estate Commission (IREC). It was created within the Professional Licensing Bureau of the Iowa Department of Commerce. See the Iowa Professional Licensing Bureau Web site for more information.

Members Of The Iowa Real Estate Commission The IREC is made up of seven members, each residing in a different Iowa county. The appointments are made by the governor and confirmed by the Iowa State Senate. For representational input, five members are Iowa real estate licensees and two are nonlicensees who represent the public.
Each of the five Iowa-licensed members of the Commission is required to have at least five years of real estate experience, the last two of which must have been in Iowa. Of the five who

are licensed, one must be licensed as a salesperson. Note, though, that should the salesperson member elect to become a licensed broker, the salesperson is allowed to finish the term on the Commission but is not eligible for reappointment as a licensed real estate salesperson. There is no requirement that any members be brokers.

Commission members are not allowed to hold any elective or appointive state or federal office simultaneously with their Commission term because of potential conflicts of interest or appearances of impropriety. To conduct business, a majority of Commission members constitutes a quorum.
Appointments are for three years. No member is allowed to serve more than three consecutive terms, or nine years, total.

As with most organizations, other people help facilitate internal operations and perform the day-to-day work. The administrator of the Professional Licensing Bureau is empowered to hire and provide staff to assist the Commission with implementing the law.

The executive officer of the IREC plays a crucial role in the administration and implementation of Iowa's Real Estate Commission policy. Also, the education director plays a vital role in the implementation of the state's real estate educational requirements.
Responsibilities Of The Iowa Real Estate Commission

IREC's Web site is www.state.ia.us/irec. According to "About the Real Estate Commission" on the site, "the mission of the IREC is to protect the public through the examination, licensing, and regulation of real estate brokers, salespersons, and firms pursuant" to the following:

i: Iowa Code Chapter 543B, "Real Estate Brokers and Salespersons"
Iowa Code Chapter 543C, "Sales of Subdivided Land Outside of Iowa"
Iowa Code Chapter 557A, "Iowa Time-Share Act"
Iowa Code Chapter 558A, "Real Estate Disclosures"

b.x: The IREC mission further states that "the Commission is a policy-making body with authority to promulgate rules for the regulation of the real estate industry consistent with all applicable statutes. Rules promulgated by the Commission are published under Iowa Administrative Code Chapter 193E," and these procedural rules have the force of law. Click here to access Chapter 193E.
The Code of Iowa can only be changed by a vote of the Legislature, signed by the governor. On the other hand, from time to time, the Commission may change the rules.

The Code of Iowa, Chapter 543B, and Administrative Code, Chapter 193E, define who must hold a real estate license and who is exempt from licensing in Iowa. They also include the requirements and procedures for obtaining and renewing a real estate license.

Persons Required To Hold A Real Estate License In Iowa, a real estate license is required when someone, with the intent or upon the promise of compensation, attempts to perform or performs the services of a licensee, whether as a part of a

transaction or as an entire transaction, or claims to be a licensee. The state takes this authority under the concept of police power—that is, the right of the governing body to enact laws to protect the public. A real estate agent is in a position to assist or harm the public; hence the need for licensing.

The most important exception is people who act on their own behalf. People can list, buy, rent, or sell their own property. The state does not regulate such a transaction; owners who make a mistake may only blame themselves and no one else. Also, by extension, anyone who is employed by the owner of the property (on a regular full-time basis) is exempt from having to be licensed to buy, sell, or manage property owned, rented, leased, or to be acquired by this owner.
The following employees are also exempt from the licensing requirements:

i: Resident apartment managers when the resident manager resides in the dwelling and is engaged in the leasing of real property in connection with their employment
Government employees while conducting official duties
Those employed by a public or private utility performing real estate duties with reference to property owned, leased, or to be acquired by the employing utility

b.x: Other exemptions to the licensing requirements include the following:

i: Those acting under the authorized authority of a power of attorney instrument (attorney-in-fact) are exempt when they are acting on behalf of the owner or lessor to authorize the final consummation and execution of any contract for the sale, lease, or exchange of real estate. The exemption does not apply to someone who makes repeated and successive transactions of a like character for compensation.
Licensed attorneys admitted to practicing law in Iowa are excluded as long as the real estate transaction is solely incidental to the practice of law
Executors of wills and administrators assigned as a result of intestate estates are exempt, as are those acting as trustees in a bankruptcy

Auctioneers may advertise real property and cry the property at auction without a license. However, if the auctioneer attempts to close or closes the sale, a license is required. In addition, unlicensed auctioneers must provide in any advertising the name and address of the real estate broker or attorney who is going to be responsible for closing the sale. The real estate broker providing brokerage services must be present at the time of the auction or face a possible civil penalty of $2,500.
Isolated real estate rental transactions by an owner's representative (on behalf of the owner), as long as the acts are not repetitive
The sale of time-share uses as defined in Section 557A.2

secs.h: Recognition Of Licensure In Other States

b.x: Iowa recognizes licensure in other states.

Reciprocity agreements exist between states that have licensing requirements similar to those in Iowa and where similar recognition and courtesies are extended to each other. (See 543B.22 Nonresident's Place of Business.) Licensed nonresidents in these reciprocity states may be granted an Iowa license without having to pass Iowa's examination. (It is important to note that these agreements change from time to time. For complete, current regulations, contact the specific state regulatory body.)
However, the rules state that the licensee's brokerage must have an active place of business within the home state and that the requesting licensee's broker must have a valid Iowa license.
In addition, the applicant must prove "active" licensure (by examination) in the reciprocity state with no charges pending against the applicant.

The licensee must complete an application form, sign an affidavit indicating familiarity with Iowa license law, and sign an irrevocable consent that lawsuits and actions may be brought against licensee in the proper court of any Iowa county in which a cause of action may arise. Simply stated, if a legal action is initiated, the licensee cannot request a change of venue. (See 543B.23 Actions Against Nonresidents.)

If the home-state license of a nonresident Iowa licensee is revoked or suspended, the licensee must notify the IREC within 15 days of the adverse action taken against the real estate license. A hearing may be held to determine whether similar disciplinary action should be taken against the reciprocity licensee in Iowa.

A partnership, association, or corporation is not granted a license unless every member and/or employee who actively participates in the brokerage business holds a real estate license. Also, at least one officer, partner, or member must hold a broker's license.

Basic Requirements For Real Estate Licensure An applicant must be at least 18 years of age. Prelicensing education and testing are required to test for the applicant's competency, and all applicants are subject to a national criminal history check through the FBI. (See 543B.15(10) Qualifications.) The applicant must include with the application a written statement by the designated broker recommending that the license be granted to the applicant.
Criminal History Check

An applicant for an initial real estate broker's or salesperson's license is subject to a national criminal history check through the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), at the applicant's expense. A fingerprint/background check packet is provided by the IREC, and after completion, is returned to the IREC with the applicant's signed waiver and a processing fee. The IREC then forwards the packet to the appropriate authorities and accepts the application once the background check has been completed and received.

The criminal history check must be completed within 210 calendar days prior to the date the license application is received by the Real Estate Commission. The results of the criminal history check are not considered a public record. Because background reports are only good for 210 days, timing is critical during the process of scheduling prelicensing classes, the PSI examination, and obtaining the background check.
Residency and Citizenship Requirements

In Iowa, there are no residency requirements or any U.S. citizenship requirement. Legal aliens can become licensed real estate agents in Iowa. An applicant may not be denied because of citizenship, sex, race, religion, marital status, or national origin, although the application form may require citizenship information. To avoid the possibility of any discrimination, Iowa law prohibits the submission of photographs with any licensure application.
There are several reasons that the Commission may deny a license under Iowa Code, Section 543B.15.

An applicant for a real estate broker's or salesperson's license who has been convicted of a felony may not be considered for licensure for at least two years after the fulfillment of any type of sentence. The applicant will not be considered for at least five years if the offense involved forgery, embezzlement, obtaining money under false pretenses, theft, arson, extortion, conspiracy to defraud or other similar offense; any offense involving moral turpitude; or other offense involving a criminal breach of fiduciary duty. Moral turpitude is conduct contrary to justice, honesty, and good morals.

The Commission may deny a real estate license to anyone who has had a professional license of any kind revoked or suspended or who has had any other form of discipline imposed, in Iowa or any other jurisdiction.
A licensee who is convicted of any of these stated offenses is required to notify the Commission within ten days of the conviction. Failure to do so is grounds for license revocation.

A person who makes a false statement of material fact on an application for a broker's or salesperson's license may be denied a license by the Commission on the grounds of the false statement or submission. Licensees found to have made such a statement may have their license suspended or revoked by the Commission on the grounds of the false statement or submission.

Finally, the Commission can deny the issuance or renewal of a license if the Commission has received notification of noncompliance from Iowa's College Student Aid Commission or upon receipt of a certificate of noncompliance from the child support recovery unit of the Department of Human Services. The Commission's executive officer is authorized to prepare and serve notice on the licensee or applicant. (See 193E—-1.8(543B).)
Fees remitted with an application for licensure are refunded if the Commission finds the applicant was not qualified for a license.

The Commission may allow for exceptions. If denied a license, the applicant has 30 days to request a discovery hearing. The IREC will consider the nature of an offense, any documented aggravating or extenuating circumstances, time lapsed, rehabilitation, treatment, and restitution performed before denying or revoking a license. (See 543B.19 License Denied—Hearing.)

The Difference Between Salesperson And Broker The practices of the real estate industry are similar to the master craftsman/apprentice system of years ago. Real estate licensees start out with a salesperson's license, working under the direct supervision of a broker. Iowa law requires that a person hold an active salesperson's license for at least 24 months before becoming eligible to receive a broker's license.

An office or branch office may have only one designated broker. When the license law refers to the person in charge of an office, it is referring to this individual. The other people in the office may hold salesperson's or broker's licenses. The designated broker may be the owner or a sales manager. The designated broker is responsible for the real estate activities conducted by the associates in that office.
Special Duties Imposed on Brokers

When sponsoring a salesperson during the salesperson's first year of licensure, sponsoring brokers must be able to demonstrate that they have the time available and experience necessary to adequately supervise an inexperienced salesperson. The broker is responsible for
ensuring that all the provided real estate-related preprinted documents and forms are legal, correct, and current. The designated broker is responsible for trust account compliance too.

Each actively licensed broker associate and salesperson must be licensed under a designated broker. In addition, a Commission rule requires that each salesperson and broker associate keep the broker fully informed. A licensee who fails to do so could be subject to disciplinary action and fined up to $2,500.

A broker associate or salesperson cannot be licensed under more than one broker during the same period. Moreover, in the situation of a licensee who hires a licensed personal assistant, both the licensee and the licensed personal assistant must be licensed under the same broker.

Qualified applicants for licensure as a salesperson must successfully complete a Commission-approved course in real estate principles and practices of at least 60 classroom or computer-based hours. The required course of study for the salesperson licensing examination consists of 60 classroom or computer-based hours of real estate principles and practices. An applicant applying for an original salesperson license must also provide evidence of successful completion of the following courses:

i: 12 hours of Developing Professionalism and Ethical Practices
12 hours of Buying Practices
12 hours of Listing Practices

b.x: This education is in addition to the 60-hour salesperson prelicense course.
The applicant must complete all 96 hours of the required education during the 12 months prior to date of licensure application.

In addition, all salespersons, as a requirement of license renewal and to maintain active status, must complete a minimum of 36 hours of approved courses (to include 8 hours on legislative updates, 4 hours on ethics, and 24 hours on elective topics) during the three calendar years of the license term. The continuing education must be completed for each new license term. Evidence of compliance is required at the testing site to prove that the required prelicensing education was completed. The passing results of the examination are valid until the last working day of the sixth calendar month. During this same period, examinees must interview and find sponsoring brokers.

Additional Requirements To Become A Broker The broker candidate must be actively licensed as a salesperson for at least 24 months. Qualified applicants for a broker's license must complete a Commission-approved course of at least 72 classroom hours. This curriculum consists of nine different course subjects that must be taken within a two-year period prior to taking the broker's examination.

Each course is eight hours in length. The nine courses are as follows: Contract Law and Contract Writing, Iowa Real Estate Trust Accounts, Principles of Appraising and Market Analysis, Real Estate Law and Agency Law, Real Estate Finance, Federal and State Laws Affecting Iowa Practice, Real Estate Office Organization, Real Estate Office Administration, and Human Resources Management.
Also, applicants for an initial broker's license are subject to a national criminal history check through the FBI.
Exam Administration

A Commission-contracted provider conducts the real estate examination. Psychological Services, Inc. (PSI) holds the current contract (which is subject to change). PSI offers computerized testing through a network of testing centers. The test consists of 120 questions: 40 relate to Iowa licensing laws, and 80 are pertinent to general real estate principles and practices and is known as the national portion. Salespersons are required to score 70 percent on each portion of the test, while broker candidates are required to score 75 percent on each portion of the test.

The computerized examination is designed to establish the competency of the applicant in order to protect the interests of the public. As long as the Commission provides a uniform, standardized exam, the Commission is required to provide the examinees only their overall score plus a breakdown of the number of correct answers in each subject area.
Exam Fees
The candidate pays the examination fee directly to the testing service. The Commission establishes with the testing service the examination fees based on administration costs.
Exam Retakes

A person who fails to pass is allowed to retake the exam by going online to www.psiexams.com and paying a new examination fee. In Iowa, there is no limit on the number of times an applicant may take the examination.

What Happens After Passing The Real Estate Exam On successful completion of the exam, the applicant receives, at the test site, a passing notice and a Commission-approved application. Candidates who pass the exam must file for a license with the Commission no later than the last working day of the sixth calendar month following the qualifying examination; otherwise, the passing test results are nullified and the exam must be retaken.

Fingerprinting is required. Applicants authorize the release of a criminal background check to the IREC, which must be completed within 210 calendar days prior to the date the license application is received by the Commission.
In addition to the completed application form, the application package to the IREC must include the following:

i: Application signed by the sponsoring broker
The passing notice
Proof of the required education

Proof of errors and omissions (E&O) insurance (As a condition of licensure, all real estate licensees except those holding inactive licenses must carry E&O insurance covering all activities contemplated under Iowa license law.)
Appropriate licensure fee

secs.h: Real Estate License Term And Fees

b.x: The Commission sets fees for licensing based on the administrative costs of sustaining the Commission. Included in those costs are the per diem, expenses, and travel allowance for
Commission members. Also included are office facilities, supplies, and equipment; staff assistance; and establishment and maintenance of a real estate education program.

In 2012, the license fee charged for a three-year salesperson's license (with the year issued as the first year) is $125. A three-year broker's license is $170. A firm license is $170, and a branch office license is $50. Payment with a bad check is considered fraud.

All licenses (including inactive licenses) are issued for three-year terms, counting the remaining portion of the year issued as the first year. All individual licenses expire on December 31 of the third year of licensure.

First-time license applicants are not allowed to file for an "inactive" license. The applicant must first receive an active license that may be placed on inactive status at a later date. Individuals whose licenses are on inactive status with the IREC are not required to carry errors and omissions insurance, but they are required to renew their license every three years.

Licensees must complete 36 approved continuing education hours during their licensing term. At least 12 hours of continuing education must be taken in the classroom; so up to 24 hours may be taken by correspondence or home study.

To meet the requirements of license renewal and to maintain active status, all licensees must complete a minimum of 36 hours of approved courses. The continuing education must be completed during the three calendar years of the license term and cannot be carried over to
another license term. Approved courses in the following subjects must be completed to renew to active status: 8 hours of Law Update, 4 hours of Ethics, and 24 hours of electives.

Successful completion of continuing education requires full-time attendance throughout the program, course, or activity. A student who arrives late, leaves during class, or leaves early will not receive a certificate.

When renewing, applicants must certify continuing education hours on their applications. The Commission is then authorized to verify by random audit the education claimed by the licensee. The licensee is obligated to retain documentation of attendance for the next renewal period of three years. If audited, the licensee must show proof within 30 days of the courses attended. Failure to provide the required documentation will result in the license being placed on inactive status. Filing a false affirmation is prima facie evidence of a violation of Iowa Code.

There are alternatives to attending continuing education classes for renewal purposes. A salesperson may satisfy all continuing education requirements by retaking and passing the real estate salesperson's examination during the last six months of the renewal period. Broker associates may satisfy their continuing education requirements by retaking and passing the broker's exam within the last six months of the renewal period.

Real Estate License Expiration, Renewal, And Fees Renewal applications are not mailed; instead, licensees are mailed a reminder postcard. Licensees may renew online, or they may download the renewal form as a PDF. Renewals are accepted between November 15 and January 30. However, if the licensee fails to renew by the appropriate December 31 expiration date, then the license expires. The licensee must submit
the application form with validation of E&O insurance coverage and required continuing education, and pay the appropriate renewal fee. Renewal fees are the same as original licensure fees.

The person is given a 30-day grace period to renew by paying a $25 reinstatement fee in addition to the regular renewal fee. However, because the license expired on December 31, no real estate business can be conducted until a new "active" license is issued. In other words, the purpose of the grace period is to renew, but not to act.

If a bad check is received for renewal of a license and a replacement check is not filed by December 31, a penalty fee is added to the unpaid renewal fee. If the renewal and penalty fees are not filed with the Commission by January 30 following the expiration of the license, the license issued for the new term will be deemed null and void.
A salesperson who completes 72 hours of broker education, passes the broker's exam, and applies for and receives a broker's license does not have to renew his or her salesperson's license.

secs.h: Reinstating An Expired Real Estate License

b.x: A licensee who fails to renew or file a completed renewal application by midnight January 30 of the first year following expiration may apply to reinstate the license. Within three years of expiration, the licensee can submit a completed application, accompanied by the regular renewal fee and an additional reinstatement fee of $25 for each partial or full month following expiration. From the date of expiration to the date of reinstatement, the licensee is not authorized to practice as a real estate broker in Iowa.
An application to reinstate an expired broker or salesperson license must report that the broker or the salesperson either fully satisfied all required continuing education or has retaken and

passed the broker examination. Those holding an expired license and wishing to retake the examination in lieu of taking the continuing education hours must obtain written authorization from the Commission to show at the examination site.

The Iowa Code includes procedures that licensees must follow when transferring their license from real one real estate firm to another. The Code also includes rules licensees must follow when selling their own property, with or without assistance from their broker. Also, many licensees hire personnel to assist them in conducting real estate business. The assistants may, or may not, have a real estate license, and the Iowa Code defines the rules governing activities that assistants may provide.
Each licensee is responsible for maintaining active licensure and for fulfilling renewal duties.

Transfer Of Licensee From One Brokerage Firm To Another Normally, when a licensee is discharged by an affiliated broker or the licensee terminates the employment of or association with the affiliated broker, the licensee immediately ceases all activities that require an active real estate license until such time as a new affiliated broker makes a written request for the license and the license is reassigned to the new affiliated broker. When the licensee is discharged, the broker must immediately deliver or mail the discharged person's license to the Commission. The releasing broker must make every reasonable effort to ensure that the Commission receives the license within 72 hours of the termination date.

If the licensee terminates employment, and the agent requests that the license be returned by mail immediately to the IREC, the releasing broker must make every reasonable effort to ensure that the Commission receives the license within 72 hours of the termination date.

The IREC also offers an immediate transfer of license using a required transfer form. The immediate license transfer process involves three steps, and each step must be correctly completed in the proper order to qualify as a valid transfer.

i: Step 1. The transferring licensee must obtain certain identifying information and the signature of a new employing or affiliating broker.

Step 2. If a new affiliating broker has completed and signed step 1 of the form, the releasing broker must sign and date the transfer form and attach the old license of the transferring licensee to the form. The releasing broker must retain copies of records to demonstrate compliance with Iowa Code, Section 543B.33.

Step 3. The transferring licensee must sign the transfer form, certifying that the information on the form is true and correct and acknowledging that providing false information is a violation of Iowa Code that might result in disciplinary action against the license.

b.x: After all three steps are completed, the new affiliating broker returns the completed form and old license to the Commission. If the form and license are returned by mail, the new affiliating broker makes every reasonable effort to ensure that the Commission receives the completed form and old license within 72 hours. If all three steps to the transfer are completed in the required order, the effective date of the transfer will be the date of release from the releasing broker. And, if all transfer steps are completed in the required order, the transferring licensee may begin working immediately and is not required to wait until a new license has been issued to the new affiliated broker.

Required Disclosure For Licensees To Buy/sell Property For Their Own Portfolio With proper disclosure, it is legal for licensees to buy and/or sell property for their own benefit. However, licensees are not allowed by Commission rule to act in a dual capacity of both an agent and an undisclosed principal in any transaction. Without disclosure, there is a conflict of interest and a possible appearance of impropriety. Before buying, selling, or leasing real estate in Iowa, licensees must give written disclosure to all parties of any ownership or interest that they have or will have in the transaction. All licensees (including inactive licensees) who list their property should include a disclosure indicating that the owner is a licensed agent. When buying property, the licensee should disclose that the purchaser is a licensed agent.

Licensees should make the disclosure at the time of or prior to their solicitation of confidential information, before an offer is made by the buyer, or before an offer is accepted by the seller. Thus, licensees are allowed to purchase property from seller-clients or sell property owned by them to buyer-clients only if the licensee includes a clearly written disclosure describing the licensee's true position to the other party.

A written disclosure is required when the licensee is either the listing agent or a buyers' agent acting on behalf of the licensee's immediate family, including a spouse, parent, child, grandparent, grandchild, brother, and sister. The rule also extends to any sale or purchase on behalf of the brokerage, organization, or business entity in which the licensee has an interest.

According to the Real Estate Brokers and Salesperson Administrative Rules (193E—7.8(543B)), the required disclosure "must be made at the time of or prior to the licensee's providing specific assistance to the party or parties to the transaction. Copies of the disclosure may be provided in person or by mail, as soon as reasonably practical. If no specific assistance is provided, disclosure shall be provided prior to the parties' forming a legally binding contract, either prior to an offer made by the buyer or tenant or prior to an acceptance by the

seller or landlord, whichever comes first. . . . Satisfactory proof of this disclosure must be produced by the licensee upon request by the Commission. Whenever a licensee is in doubt as to whether an interest, relationship, association, or affiliation requires disclosure under this rule, the safest course of action is to make the written disclosure."

Licensee Purchase Or Sale Of Property For Themselves Without Broker Participation In Iowa, without broker participation, licensed agents are allowed by Commission rule to sell their own property provided no brokerage fees are to be paid, it is strictly a "by owner" transaction, and the licensee does not function as a licensee in any capacity throughout the transaction. If all these conditions exist, then a licensee would be allowed to advertise the property without including the name of the licensee's broker.

In cases where licensees choose to sell their real property as a "by owner," any involved earnest money may be written directly to the owner/licensee. However, in this case, it would be advisable for the seller's or the buyer's attorney to hold the earnest money until the transaction closes.

Licensee Sale Of Owned Property Through Their Broker When licensees (1) list or act as an agent in the sale (lease, rental, exchange) of property owned by the licensees and (2) receive money from the purchaser, these funds must be deposited into their broker's trust account. The licensees must notify all concerned that they hold a real estate license. This applies whether or not the property is listed.

Many top producers hire support persons to assist them. These assistants may be licensed or not licensed. Any brokerage that allows an affiliated licensee to employ support personnel (personal assistants) must implement a written company policy authorizing the practice. The written policy must include the prescribed duties that the support personnel may perform on behalf of the affiliated licensee. These duties are described by Commission rule.

In Iowa, affiliated licensees who engage personal assistants have the primary responsibility for their supervision. Obviously, the firm or sponsoring broker has supervisory responsibilities for the acts or activities of personal assistants, but the primary responsibility rests with the persons who employ them. For tax purposes, personal assistants must be either independent contractors or employees.

Activities Unlicensed Assistants May Perform Under the direct supervision of a licensee, Iowa law permits unlicensed assistants to answer the telephone and provide listing information to other licensees as well as to forward calls from the public to a licensee. An unlicensed assistant can schedule an open house, perform physical maintenance, and accompany a licensee to an open house or a showing and function as a host or hostess. In addition, the unlicensed assistant is allowed to receive, record, and deposit earnest money, security deposits, and advance rents.
Unlicensed assistants may also perform the following duties:

i: Submit listing data to the multiple-listing service
Check on the status of closing files
Assemble documents for closing
Have keys made
Write advertisements
Place signs on property
Act as a courier
Schedule appointments with the seller or the seller's agent to show the property
Arrange dates and times for inspections, mortgage applications, walk-through inspections, and closings
Hand to the public preprinted property information that has been prepared by a licensee

b.x: Prohibited Activities For An Unlicensed Assistant Iowa law prohibits unlicensed assistants from using the telephone or acting in person to prospect for listings, leases, buyers, 1031 exchange candidates, or property management contracts. The procuring of prospects is by definition a function of a real estate licensee.
In addition, they are prohibited from independently hosting open houses, kiosks, home-show booths, or fairs of their licensed employers.

Showing property without the licensed employer being present is strictly prohibited. Other than the time and place of a closing, answering any real estate–related question germane to the actual transaction is prohibited. Also prohibited are any negotiations or agreements regarding commission structuring or the collecting or holding of deposit money, rent, or anything else of value from either party.

One final note, just to clarify: Unlicensed personal assistants are not allowed to hold themselves out in any manner as being licensed or affiliated with a particular firm or real estate business. In other words, they are not allowed to print their names on real estate company business cards in an attempt to deceive the public.

Iowa Real Estate Commission Grant Program The IREC used to allocate $25 from each license renewal and establish a grant program for community colleges, colleges, and universities in Iowa to create real estate degree opportunities. The program ended and the section of the administrative code that established it (543B.54) was rescinded on July 1, 2013.

The selling of chances (lotteries) by a real estate brokerage firm is illegal in Iowa. In essence, lotteries create an opportunity to collect monies that exceed the value of the property being purchased. To avoid any appearance of impropriety and to protect the public from unscrupulous sales practices, the temptation to sell chances is removed by Commission rule. Iowa, though, does allow nonprofits to sell chances as a fundraiser to purchase real estate.

Files, records, and other required documents may be stored in electronic format for convenience and efficiency in a system for electronic record storage, analysis, and retrieval. However, required records may be retained as an electronic record only if the record storage medium can be easily accessed and the records can be readily retrieved and transferred to a legible printed form upon request. The scanning or electronic generation of a record must be monitored to ensure that the copy is clear, legible, and true before the original is shredded. And once the original record is transferred to the appropriate electronic storage medium consistent with this rule, the Commission will no longer require the retention of the record in its original medium. Electronic records are considered the same as originals.

t: Iowa Brokerage Offices, Advertising and Trust Accounts

At minimum, a branch office must have at least two licenses: a designated broker's license and a branch office license.
