b.x: With a broker's license, one may open and operate a real estate business. The broker may hire persons holding either a salesperson's or associate broker's license, although the designated broker is ultimately responsible for the actions of affiliated licensees. This unit covers the additional rules and regulations for brokers regarding advertising and trust accounts. Additionally, real estate licensees must comply with state variations to federal laws. State variations to the federal Fair Housing Act and Megan's Law are noted.

Every Iowa real estate firm or self-employed broker must maintain an office for the transaction of business in the state of Iowa. The office must be open to the public during business hours or by appointment. To open and operate an office (or branch offices) requires licensing.

secs.h: Required Licenses For Opening An Office

b.x: A person planning to open a real estate office must hold a broker's license. The broker may then hire those persons holding either a salesperson's or associate broker's license to work in the office.

Real estate firms may take one of several business forms, any of which must be licensed. A partnership association, corporation, professional corporation, or limited liability company is not granted a license unless every member or officer who actively participates in the brokerage business also holds a real estate license. At least one member, called the principal broker, must hold a broker's license.

At a minimum, a branch office must have at least two licenses: a designated broker's license and a branch office license. One branch office license is issued in the name of the firm or proprietor, and one is issued in the name of the designated broker or broker associate assigned to supervise the branch office. Any number of licensees can be affiliated with the office, or there can be just the broker.

Brokers are required to supervise all advertising and verify the accuracy of the materials. If the broker discovers an error or a violation of the rules (193E) or the law (543B), the broker is required to correct the issue within ten calendar days or as soon as is possible.

In Iowa, a blind ad is one in which brokerage firms or listing agents include just their own name, a post office box number, or a telephone number to possibly deceive readers into believing that the property is advertised by a private party. This unscrupulous practice is illegal.

All brokers, when advertising real estate, must use their regular business name, or name under which the broker is licensed, and unmistakably indicate that the party is a real estate broker and not a private party. Real estate advertising must be honest. It should never be misleading, deceptive, or intentionally misrepresent any property, terms, values, or policies and services of the brokerage.
Real Estate Office Internet Advertising
Iowa Code includes special requirements for a real estate office to advertise on the Internet. Iowa requires all the following disclosures on each page of the firm's Web site:

i: The firm's name as registered with the Commission (abbreviations not permitted)
The city and state in which the firm's main office is located
Those states where the firm holds a brokerage license

b.x: Real Estate Licensee Internet Advertising
Licensees who advertise or market real estate on personal Web sites must include on each page controlled by their Web site the following information:

i: The licensee's name
The name of the firm with which the licensee is affiliated (abbreviations not permitted)
The city and state in which the licensee's office is located
The states in which the licensee holds a broker's or salesperson's license

b.x: Internet Chat Room, E-mail, and Discussion Groups

To ensure a level playing field, many states, including Iowa, require that real estate firms that use any Internet electronic communication, such as e-mail, bulletin boards, or e-mail discussion groups, to advertise or market property include certain disclosures on the first or last page. These disclosures include the firm's name as registered with the Commission, the city and state in which the firm's main office is located, and those states where the firm holds a brokerage license.

For licensees who use personal e-mail, bulletin boards, or e-mail discussion groups to advertise or market property, Commission rules state that they must include on the first or last page a business-card-like identity disclosure. The disclosure must include the licensee's name; the affiliated firm's name, as registered with the Commission; the city and state in which the licensee's office is located; and the states in which the licensee holds a broker's or salesperson's license.

A broker may place a For Sale or For Rent sign on a property only with the written permission of the owner. Based on the legal theory of undue enrichment, failure to remove a sign when requested violates IREC rule and is subject to disciplinary action in the form of a civil penalty. After a sold listing closes, the new owner must consent to leave a Sold sign in place.

Trust money is money that belongs to someone else, and it is common practice in real estate sales transactions for a broker to hold money for the buyer. Every Iowa-based real estate brokerage firm that expects to handle funds belonging to others must maintain a common trust account, identified by the word "trust."

Brokers that receive or expect to receive trust funds must file a written Consent to Examine and Audit Trust Account form that irrevocably authorizes the Commission to examine and audit the trust account. The form includes the account name and number and the name and address of the depository. However, a broker who no longer expects to receive trust funds may file an affidavit with the Commission and close the account.

Trust account funds must be deposited in federally insured institutions (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation or National Credit Union Administration) located in Iowa. The depository can be a federally insured bank, savings association, savings bank, or credit union.
Timing of the Deposits

All funds belonging to others, except those agreed to between contracting parties, must be deposited into the broker's trust account no later than five banking days after the last signature of acceptance. This dated instrument can be an offer to purchase, a rental agreement, a lease, an exchange, or even an option. However, before obtaining the last signature, it is customary to keep earnest money checks in the transaction file of the listing broker.
Deposits Involving a Cooperative Sale

In the case of a cooperative sale, when one office has the listing, and another office is working with the buyer, the listing broker usually elects to close the transaction and have the buyer's agent make the earnest money check payable to the listing firm's trust account. The reason for doing it this way is because the listing broker is legally responsible for the closing even though the closing may be completed by another licensee. If cash is received by a cooperative buyer's agent, the buyer's agent can either convert it to a money order or deposit the cash into the buyer's broker's trust account and then issue a check to the listing company's trust account. The reason for the rule is to leave a paper trail to properly account for the cash received.
Deposits Involving a Build-to-order Purchase Agreement

On a build-to-order purchase agreement, the buyer and the builder might possibly agree that the builder should hold the earnest money deposit rather than the broker. The buyer and the builder could treat the earnest money as collateral for building on the buyer's owned real estate. Whenever licensees are in doubt as to whether funds received should be deposited into their broker's trust account, the safest course of action is to deposit those funds into the broker's trust account.
Deposits Other Than Cash or Check

In Iowa, postdated checks or anything other than cash or an immediately cashable check are not to be accepted as earnest money unless that fact is so communicated to the seller prior to the acceptance of the offer and is so stated in the offer to purchase.
Iowa Code includes rules pertaining to interest on deposits in trust accounts.

Unless there is a written agreement between all parties to the contrary, trust accounts in Iowa are required to be interest-bearing. The interest on the account is transferred quarterly to the treasurer of the state and then transferred to the department of economic development for deposit in the local housing assistance program fund.
Money belonging to others may not be invested in any type of fixed maturity account, security, or certificate without the written consent of the party or parties to whom the money belongs.
By Commission rule, in no event may an Iowa broker be paid interest earned on monies held in trust for others by the broker.

On a calendar quarterly basis, the depository or the broker transfers the interest to the treasurer of the state. The depository name should read "Iowa Finance Authority" and the federal tax information number (TIN) 52-1699886 should be on the 1099 reporting form when reporting the interest to the IRS. The depository should send the 1099 reporting form to Iowa Finance Authority, 2015 Grand Avenue, Des Moines, IA 50312. The interest is used to fund housing assistance programs.

With a written agreement between the buyer and the seller, a separate, interest-bearing trust account may be created for their benefit. However, it must be separate from the trust account that bears interest payable to the State of Iowa. Interest is disbursed at the time of settlement, and service charges for this separate trust account are considered a business expense to the broker and not deductible from the proceeds. (See 193E-13.1(2)g.)
By definition, commingling is mixing personal funds with those belonging to other people. A broker should not mix personal funds with trust deposits from real estate transactions.

However, the State of Iowa allows brokerage firms to open trust accounts using personal funds not to exceed $500. The $500 is used to cover trust account service charges and the purchase of trust account checks. At no time can trust monies be used to cover service charges. On notification that the broker's personal funds are insufficient to cover service charges, the broker has up to 15 days to make a deposit to correct the deficiency. A broker's equity ledger (personal funds) is required to monitor this account.

Any amount in excess of $500 is considered commingling. (See 193E-13.1(1)c.) The problem with excess personal funds in the broker's trust account is simple. If the broker were to commingle personal funds into this account and the IRS froze the broker's accounts, then the trust account also would be frozen. The same thing could happen if a sole proprietor owned the brokerage and the sole proprietor suddenly died after commingling personal funds with the trust account. The commingled brokerage trust account could end up in probate. In either event, all closings would be tied up for a considerable length of time. To avoid these potential problems, brokers may not keep more than $500 in this account.
General Procedure for Disbursing Trust Funds
As a rule, no funds can be disbursed from the trust account before the closing without the informed written consent of all the parties.

In the event of a dispute over the return or forfeiture of any earnest money or escrow deposit held by the broker, the broker is required to hold the deposit in the trust account until one of the following conditions is met:

1. A written consent is received from both parties. 2. A final judgment of the court is received. 3. A final decision of a binding alternative dispute resolution is received. 4. A civil court action is filed by one or more of the parties, at which time the broker may request to pay the deposit or escrow funds into the court.

Also, anytime a broker in good faith believes that neither party will agree on the disposition of the deposit or file a civil court action to determine its disposition, then the broker may elect to file an interpleader action with the appropriate court and pay the disputed deposit into the court.
Unclaimed Trust Funds
Unclaimed trust funds are paid to the treasurer of the State of Iowa.
Funds That May Not Be Paid Directly Out of the Trust Account

Brokers should never use a trust account as their business operating account or for personal uses. Monies that may not be disbursed directly from this account include salaries and normal business or operational expenses. The broker may pay company commissions or commissions to other companies from the trust account.
An Example of Money In and Out of a Trust Account

It is possible for a broker to place an earnest money deposit into the trust account and at closing, with written permission, transfer the earnest money to the brokerage account in lieu of commission earned. For example, a broker lists a $10,000 lot for a 10 percent commission. It sells for full price, and a check for $1,000 earnest money is written and deposited into the broker's trust account.

At closing, the owner of the property gives the broker written permission to keep the $1,000 earnest money (located in the trust account) in lieu of the commission owed. The $1,000 earnest money held in the trust account, due and payable now as commission earned, must be promptly withdrawn and transferred to the broker's business account from the broker's trust account, or the broker might be found guilty of unlawful commingling.

Distributing Earnest Money When The Buyer And Seller Disagree Under certain conditions, the broker is authorized to release disputed earnest money without written consent. One example is when the broker is in receipt of a final judgment of the court directing the disposition of the deposit or there is a final decision of a binding alternative dispute resolution. Another example is when a civil action is filed to determine the disposition of the earnest money, at which time the broker may seek court authorization to pay the deposit into the court (an interpleader action).

Also, in the absence of a pending civil action or written agreement, brokers are allowed to disburse disputed earnest money to buyers or lessees based on good-faith decisions that contingencies have not been met. This rule requires that before disbursement, the broker must
give 30 days' written notice by certified mail to all concerned parties at their last known mailing addresses, setting forth the broker's proposed action and the grounds for the decision.

For example, a buyer makes an offer to a seller subject to the sale of the buyer's home on or before March 3. The buyer includes a $2,000 earnest money check with the offer, and the seller accepts the buyer's offer. The buyer's home doesn't sell by March 3, and therefore a written request for the return of the buyer's earnest money is initiated. The seller, for no valid reason, decides not to cooperate and refuses to sign the written release form. At this point, the broker is allowed to make a good-faith decision that the contingency (subject to sale) has not been met and initiate the return of the $2,000 earnest money to the buyer by serving a 30-day certified mail written notice to both parties. During the required 30-day waiting period, the seller can take legal action to prevent the broker's good-faith decision from being carried out.

Also, in the absence of a pending lawsuit or written agreement, when six months from the date of the dispute have passed, it is not grounds for disciplinary action when if a broker disburses the earnest money to a seller or a landlord in a transaction based on a good-faith decision that the buyer, the renter, or the lessee failed to perform as agreed. This rule requires that before disbursement the broker give 30 days' written notice by certified mail to all concerned parties at their last known mailing addresses, setting forth the broker's proposed action and the grounds for the decision.

A written release is not required when sellers reject an offer or, before notification of acceptance, buyers withdraw their offer. In both events, the earnest money is returned to the buyer without delay. In Iowa, it is customary for licensees to keep earnest money checks in their transaction files until offer acceptance. If the offer does not result in a contract, then the earnest money check is simply returned to the buyer or the tenant.

Rules Governing Earnest Money And Commissions If a buyer and a seller agree, just before closing, to rescind the contract, a broker may not take commission fees directly from the trust account, even if the broker feels the commission was earned. Should a transaction fail to consummate, under no circumstances is the broker entitled to withhold any portion of the earnest money, even though a commission is earned.

For example, the sellers accept an offer for the sale of their home accompanied by a $2,000 earnest money check. After acceptance, the buyers ask the sellers to let them out of the contract because of an unexpected job transfer. The owners agree and tell the buyers they can have their earnest money back, too. In this case, when the sellers accepted the buyers' offer, a commission was earned; however, the listing broker cannot hold the buyers' and the sellers' earnest money hostage. The broker must return the earnest money as directed and look to the sellers for compensation for services rendered.

Brokerage firms in Iowa are required to maintain a two-journal record-keeping (trust account) system. The first is called a general ledger account, which records in chronological order all receipts and disbursements. The second is called an individual ledger account (clearly separate from the general ledger), which identifies in chronological order all receipts and disbursements for every individual transaction.

For receipts, both journals must include the date, the name of the depositor, the name of the principal or property identification, the check number, and the amount deposited. For disbursements, both journals must include the date, the name of payee, the name of the principal or property identification, the check number, and the amount disbursed.

The purpose of the two-journal record-keeping system is to provide a means for monthly reconciliation. The general ledger account balance at the end of each month should mirror both the bank's balance and the total balances of all the individual ledger accounts.

Individual ledger accounts also alert brokers when an account is low on funds. It prevents the broker from spending more money than what is in the individual account. Without individual ledger accounts, brokers could unknowingly use someone else's trust funds to pay out on another account.
Property Management Security Deposits

Pursuant to a written property management or rental agreement, receipts from property management and/or rental account transactions may be deposited into a separate non-interest-bearing trust account. If agreed to as part of the property management agreement a consent-to-examine form is not required.

If deposits are separately maintained in non-interest-bearing trust accounts, then not less than annually, the broker must provide a complete accounting of all monies received and disbursed from the accounts.
Tenants' Security Deposits

Property management trust accounts require individual ledger accounts for each tenant. These individual ledgers must identify each tenant's rental unit and security deposit, and show all receipts and disbursements together with check number and date.

secs.h: Trust Fund Rules For Farm Managers

b.x: If agreed to as part of a farm management agreement, a consent-to-examine form is not required for a separate farm business operating trust account in the name of the owner. The same is true for a separate property management account in the name of the owner.

The state agency that handles fair housing complaints is the Iowa Civil Rights Commission. Iowa Code, Sections 216.8 and 216.8A detail the protections in Iowa housing. The purpose of this Commission is to enforce civil rights laws, increase public awareness of civil rights, provide dispute resolution services, and offer community services throughout the state. There is no charge for filling out a complaint form. If federal law covers the same situation, the Commission will cross-file the complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). A complaint must be filed with the Commission within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory incident. Complaints must be filed with HUD within one year, or private court action can be filed within two years.

During the process, the parties sometimes decide to settle the case through mediation. If the case is not resolved, the complaint is investigated. When the investigation is complete, an administrative law judge determines whether there is reasonable cause to believe discrimination occurred. If the judge finds it has, each party has 20 days to choose a course of action. They can then proceed in district court, or they can continue with the public hearing process through the Commission.
For more information, please visit the Iowa Civil Rights Commission's Web site at www.state.ia.us/government/crc.
Iowa and Federal fair housing laws
The Iowa fair housing law is similar to the federal fair housing laws.

For housing discrimination issues, Iowa's protected classes include the following: race, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, national origin, mental disability, physical disability, and familial status (presence of children in the home)(Iowa Civil Rights Code 216.8, Unfair or Discriminatory Practices—Housing) for more information. Municipalities and counties may add protected categories too (e.g., age).

Briefly, Megan's Law requires that certain sex offenders, when released from prison, register with the local authorities where they live. Iowa law poses no burden on a real estate licensee to discover or disclose the presence of a sex offender. According to Iowa law, if an offender is 1) required to register in the State of Iowa and 2) has been convicted of an "aggravated offense against a minor," the offender is prohibited from residing within 2,000 feet of real property comprising a school or child care facility. Seewww.iowasexoffender.com/faq/content.

The Iowa Competition Law is constructed to complement and comply with federal antitrust laws, such as the Sherman Antitrust Act, the Clayton Antitrust Act, and the Robinson-Patman Amendments. The purpose of the Iowa Competition Law is to help achieve uniform application of state and federal laws, which collectively prohibit restraints of economic activity and monopolistic practices. One aspect of these laws deals with unlawful agreements allocating customers or markets, thus refraining from healthy competition for each other's business. In real estate, tying arrangements violate this aspect of the law.
A licensee participating in any of the practices described in the Iowa Code Section 543B.29(3) are deemed to be engaging in unethical conduct and a practice harmful or detrimental to the public.

Often called tying agreements (or tying arrangements), these are illegal actions under which agreements to purchase one property are allegedly "tied" to the use or purchase of another service or product allowing the licensee to collect a commission on a transaction for which no work was done.

The purpose of 543B.60A Prohibited Practices is to prohibit licensee practices that interfere with contractual arrangements, place improper restrictions on consumer choice, compromise a licensee's fiduciary obligations, and create conflicts of interest. Here are several examples:

i: Any requirement, in connection with the sale of a building lot, that the licensee receive from the homebuilder an exclusive right to list any home built for speculation on the lot
Any agreement to sell lots on behalf of a developer on the bogus condition that the developer require prospective homebuilders to list their homes, which were built for speculation, with the licensee
In connection with the sale of a lot to a consumer or homebuilder, any requirement to pay a full commission on the value of the property to be constructed on the lot
A condition under which the purchasers of a home are required to list their current home with the licensee
In connection with the sale of a lot to a consumer, a requirement that the consumer must use a specified homebuilder or lender
Any requirement that a mortgage broker, bank, savings and loan, or other financial institution require a customer to pay a commission to a real estate licensee in order to obtain a loan
Any requirement that a licensee affiliated with a lending institution be used as a real estate agent in order to obtain the benefits of the lending institution

cloze.s: Also, in the absence of a pending lawsuit or written agreement, when _____ from the date of the dispute have passed, it is not grounds for disciplinary action when if a broker disburses the earnest money to a seller or a landlord in a transaction based on a good-faith decision that the buyer, the renter, or the lessee failed to perform as agreed.
cloze.full: Also, in the absence of a pending lawsuit or written agreement, when six months from the date of the dispute have passed, it is not grounds for disciplinary action when if a broker disburses the earnest money to a seller or a landlord in a transaction based on a good-faith decision that the buyer, the renter, or the lessee failed to perform as agreed.

cloze.s: This rule requires that before disbursement the broker give _____' written notice by certified mail to all concerned parties at their last known mailing addresses, setting forth the broker's proposed action and the grounds for the decision.
cloze.full: This rule requires that before disbursement the broker give 30 days' written notice by certified mail to all concerned parties at their last known mailing addresses, setting forth the broker's proposed action and the grounds for the decision.

cloze.s: For example, the sellers accept an offer for the sale of their home accompanied by a _____ earnest money check.
cloze.full: For example, the sellers accept an offer for the sale of their home accompanied by a $2,000 earnest money check.

cloze.s: A complaint must be filed with the Commission within _____ of the alleged discriminatory incident.
cloze.full: A complaint must be filed with the Commission within 300 days of the alleged discriminatory incident.

cloze.s: Complaints must be filed with HUD within one year, or private court action can be filed within _____.
cloze.full: Complaints must be filed with HUD within one year, or private court action can be filed within two years.

cloze.s: If the judge finds it has, each party has _____ to choose a course of action.
cloze.full: If the judge finds it has, each party has 20 days to choose a course of action.

i: Depending on the situation, the licensee may be representing a buyer, a seller, a landlord, a tenant, a property owner, or more than one party in a transaction.
Agency duties are governed by common law and statutory law.
In Iowa, agents' duties to their client include care, loyalty, obedience, accounting and disclosure.
A licensee may perform ministerial acts that are not considered client-level duties.
A broker works for a client and with a customer.
Agency relationships may be single, dual, special, general, and designated.
Dual agency must be created with the written consent of the client.
Brokerage agreements may take several forms.
All buyer-brokerage agreements must be in writing and contain statements disclosing the brokerage policy on cooperating with and compensating other brokerages.
Iowa law requires brokerage agreements to include four specific requirements known as minimum services.
The broker enters into employment agreements with the licensees who work for the broker permitting the licensees to act as agents for the broker.
Procuring cause means that a licensee started or caused a chain of events that resulted in the sale of a listed property.
Any commission or fee in any brokerage agreement is fully negotiable among the parties to that brokerage agreement.
The broker is required to deposit all funds received on behalf of the owner into the broker's trust account.
All listing contracts in Iowa must be written and properly identify the property and the terms and conditions under which the property is to be sold.
A broker protection clause can be included in either the listing or the buyer brokerage agreement and extends beyond the expiration of the agreement.
It is illegal to place a sign on any property offering it for sale, rent, or lease without the owner's consent.
Referral fees are legal if paid between brokers.
The taking of a net listing is considered unprofessional conduct and constitutes a violation of the Iowa Code.
Agents are not allowed to solicit listings with another brokerage that have not been terminated.
Listing and brokerage agreements may not be assigned, sold, or otherwise transferred to another broker without the express written consent of all the parties to the original agreement.

b.x: Most real estate licensees engage in brokerage that involves bringing together two consumers—buyer and seller or landlord and tenant—to enter into a contract to sell, buy, rent, or manage real property in exchange for a fee. When brokerage is practiced, agency relationships are created and the state regulates the actions by the broker and any affiliated
licensees who work with the consumer. Depending on the circumstance, the brokerage may work for (be an agent of ) a consumer/client or work with a consumer/customer.

Because consumers rely on real estate licensees for information, it is imperative that consumers understand the type of agency representation, if any, they have with the real estate licensee. This unit deals with Iowa agency concepts, agency disclosures, brokerage agreements, and antitrust laws.

In real estate transactions, agency means a relationship in which a real estate broker acts for or represents another by the other person's express authority in a transaction. The relationship is built on mutual respect, trust, honesty, and promise keeping. To create an agency relationship, one party, the client (also called the principal), delegates authority to an agent, who, in return, consents to act for that client. Real estate licensees choose to either accept or refuse a seller's or a buyer's overture to become an agent. As long as the refusal isn't based on discrimination, it is an agent's prerogative to either accept or refuse to take a listing or work with a particular buyer.

The agency relationship between a licensee and the parties involved in a real estate transaction may take many forms. Depending on the situation, the licensee may be representing a buyer, a seller, a landlord, a tenant, a property owner or more than one party in a transaction. The agency relationship created with these parties may be a single agency, dual agency, or designated agency. The agency may also be referred to a special or a general agency, depending on the duties assigned to the agent by the client.

In the case of a seller-client, the seller might elect to sell the home without the services of an agent, but instead, elect to delegate the task to an agent. The agent receives (from the seller) express authority to procure a buyer, and by written authority, receives permission to put up a sign, use a lockbox system (in the owner's absence) to gain entry into the home, and be present during offer negotiations. However, the agent does not have authority to bind the seller to an offer.
Under Iowa Code, Section 543B.63, a licensee is not considered a subagent of a client of another licensee solely by reason of membership or other affiliation by the licensee in a multiple
listing service or other similar information source, and an offer of subagency must not be made through a multiple listing service or other similar information source.
Sources of Agency Law

Once an agency relationship is created, the licensee owes certain duties to the client, in addition to the duties owed to a customer. Iowa rules of agency require the placement of the client's interest ahead of the interests of any other party to the transaction.

Agency duties are governed by common law (the rules established by tradition and court decisions) and statutory law (the laws enacted by state legislatures and governing bodies like the Iowa Real Estate Commission [IREC]). Additionally, today many courts also include the National Association of REALTORS® Code of Ethics as a guideline, even if the licensee is not a REALTOR®. The combination of these three defines the rights and duties of the parties. However, if the statutory rules conflict with the traditional laws of agency, then the rules supersede tradition.
Agency Duties

In Iowa, the agent is obligated to place the client's interest ahead of the interest of any other party (loyalty), unless doing so violates the law. The Iowa agent must also disclose to the client all information known by the licensee that is material to the transaction and that is not known to the client or could not be discovered by the client through a reasonably diligent inspection. The agent must also disclose any financial interests the brokerage has in the transaction. The agent must fulfill the instructions (obedience) within the scope of the agency agreement (unless they
are unlawful instructions). Finally, the Iowa agent may not accept any fees from anyone other than the client without full disclosure to all parties.

A seller's agent who helps the seller arrive at a realistic listing price, develop a marketing plan, and negotiate offers demonstrates reasonable care. A buyer's agent demonstrates reasonable care by helping the buyer evaluate property values, financial alternatives, and any offers and counteroffers.

The duty of accounting requires the recording and reporting of all funds received from or on behalf of the principal. State law also requires that these funds be deposited into the broker's trust account within five banking days after the date on the document identifying receipt of the last signature of acceptance. Obviously, as previously mentioned, commingling is illegal, as is conversion. (Conversion is the practice of spending commingled funds for personal use.)
Unauthorized Practice of Law

By legal definition, a real estate broker in Iowa prepares offers to purchase, listing contracts, agency disclosure forms, real property and agricultural rental agreements, commercial rental agreements of one year or less, and groundwater hazard statements, including any addendums, modifications, or amendments to these documents. Working outside of this definition could be considered the unauthorized practice of law. Therefore, the Iowa Supreme Court requires brokers to obtain written permission from their clients to select, prepare, and complete form documents incident to a real estate transaction, identifying that these stated documents are binding legal documents and, if desired, that competent legal advice should be sought before signing.
Ministerial Acts
A licensee may perform certain acts that are not considered client-level duties.

In Iowa, ministerial acts are those acts that a licensee is allowed to perform for a consumer that are informative in nature and do not rise to the level of specific assistance. Examples of ministerial acts include responding to telephone inquiries, fielding questions at either an open house or the office, or setting appointments to view property. Other examples include accompanying an appraiser, an inspector, or a contractor on a visit to a property; referring a person to another broker or service provider; or completing factual information for a consumer on an offer. (See ministerial acts in 193E-2.1 Definitions.)

For example, let's consider the completion of factual information for a consumer on an offer. If an agent were holding an open house for a seller client and an unknown buyer attending the open house desired to write an offer, then the agent could inform the buyer that the agent was solely representing the owner. In other words, while able to complete and present the offer for the buyer, the agent would not be the buyer's agent. However, if the buyer desired representation, a different agent could be found for that purpose. If not, then the buyer in this situation would be considered a nonclient and any information that the buyer wished to remain confidential shouldn't be shared with the listing agent.
The Customer in a Real Estate Transaction

A customer is a consumer of real estate–related services who is not being represented by the licensee. It is easy to recognize who the customer is when the agent solely represents the seller. The buyer is the customer. However, if the agent solely represents the buyer, then the customer becomes the seller.

While providing brokerage services to customers, licensees must do so honestly and in good faith. They must diligently exercise reasonable skill and care, and licensees must disclose all material adverse facts that the licensee knows except those material facts that have already been discovered or discussed. In addition, there is a duty to account for any customer's property that comes into the licensee's possession. Agents do not have a duty to discover latent (hidden) defects in the property. An agent who is aware of such defects must disclose them to prospective buyers (customers).
The Client in a Real Estate Transaction

A client is a party to a transaction who has an agency agreement with the licensee for brokerage services. Another name for a client is the principal. The principal is the individual who hires and delegates authority to a broker to represent the individual's interests. The client or principal can be the seller, the landlord, the buyer, or the tenant.

In single agency, the agent represents only one party in any single transaction. The agent owes fiduciary duties exclusively to one principal, who may be either a seller/landlord or a buyer/tenant. Any third party is a customer. A customer is a consumer who is not being represented by a licensee but for whom the licensee may perform ministerial acts.

A seller's agent is an agent, sometimes called the listing agent, who singularly represents the seller in a real estate transaction. The buyer is then considered the customer. A buyer's agent is an agent, often simply called the buyer's agent, who singularly represents the buyer in a real estate transaction. In buyer agency, the seller is the customer.

Many real estate transactions in Iowa are single agency. The listing company represents the seller, and the co-op broker represents the buyer. In some offices that useappointed agency, one licensee represents the seller; another licensee in the same office represents the buyer.

Dual agency is created when both parties to a transaction give written authority to one licensee to represent both parties in the transaction. Iowa law authorizes the use of consensual, disclosed dual agency, provided the brokerage has a company policy permitting its use. The practice is illegal without informed, written authority. Dual agents carefully coordinate the entire transaction and are obligated to keep both parties' business confidential.

When the agent is hired to perform a specific task or transaction, a special agency is created. The listing agent's authority in a real estate transaction is very limited. The listing agent is a special agent—that is, one who is hired for a short term and receives limited authority. Agency agreements spell out the agency relationship.
Even if all of the terms of the listing agreement are met, and the agent may have earned a commission, the seller's agent does not have legal authority to bind the seller to an offer.

A general agency is created when the agent is empowered to represent the principal in a broad range of matters related to a particular business or activity. The general agentmay, for example, bind the principal to any contract within the scope of the agent's authority.

A property manager is typically a general agent for the owner. By the terms of the management agreement, the property manager is often given authority to bind the owner in a lease or for paying for a repair. Likewise, a licensee affiliated with the designated broker is a general agent, depending on the terms of the employment agreement. The key terms of general agency are long-term, broad authority.

In Iowa, seller-clients and buyer-clients may appoint an Iowa broker (in writing) to appoint one or more different licensees affiliated with the brokerage to exclusively represent one of them. These appointed agents work as single agents for either the seller or the buyer, to the exclusion of all other licensees in the brokerage. Therefore, two licensees (from the same real estate brokerage) end up representing opposite sides, such as the buyer and the seller, in a single real estate transaction.

Under Iowa rules, an appointed broker will not be considered a dual agent unless the broker personally represents both the buyer and the seller. Using appointed agents avoids the potential conflict of interests inherent in dual agency.

When representing parties in a real estate transaction, Iowa law requires that licensees obtain written agency disclosures. The written disclosure form, signed by the client, verifies that the agent has, in fact, discussed agency options with the client. At least an oral disclosure must be made prior to offering specific assistance. However, the written agency disclosure statement must be completed before any offer is made by the buyer/tenant or accepted by the seller/landlord.

It is important to note that just disclosing the broker's company policy does not create agency. The client must agree to an agency relationship before the agent either elicits or accepts conversation of a confidential nature that the other party may unknowingly divulge and possibly harm the party's bargaining abilities. The disclosure does not create an agency relationship that obligates the consumer to pay any compensation to a broker.

Initially, the disclosure may be oral, and through dialogue and discussion, the consumer recognizes agency options available. Written disclosure must be made before the consumer enters into any written agreement. The time frame varies, depending on whether the consumer is a seller or a buyer.

The licensee provides a written disclosure to the seller before a listing agreement is signed. Buyers must acknowledge the representation before an offer is made, and sellers must acknowledge the relationship before an offer is presented. Written disclosure forms are kept on file in the listing broker's office and the buyer's broker's office for five years.

Specific assistance is a phrase used to mean any communication beyond casual conversation about the facts and features of a property that leads to the discovery of confidential information. It refers to eliciting or accepting confidential information about someone's needs, selling or buying motivation, price range, or financial qualifications. With this knowledge, an unscrupulous agent could disclose the confidential information of a client to the other party in a real estate transaction, thereby compromising the client's bargaining position.

In Iowa, specific assistance does not mean preliminary conversations or casual talk concerning price range, location, and property styles; nor does it mean responding to general factual questions concerning properties that have been advertised for sale or lease.

A dual agent acts as an agent for both the seller and the buyer or the landlord and the tenant in the same transaction. Many offices have a policy permitting dual agency with informed written consent. In a dual agency, the licensee must endeavor to remain impartial and not aggressively represent the interest of either party to the exclusion or detriment of the other party. Licensees can act as dual agents only with written consent of all the parties.

The possibility of dual agency should be discussed and agreed to before the seller signs a listing agreement or before an agent provides specific assistance to the buyer. If the consumer creates an agency agreement with the agent and agrees to the possibility of dual agency, then a second disclosure is required at the time that the agent actually becomes a dual agent.

If an unrepresented buyer enters an open house, the seller's agent running the open house should immediately disclose that the two are working as an agent for the seller. They can offer the buyer a disclosed dual agency if the buyer agrees.

Agency disclosures do not include agreements for broker compensation. The obligation of either the seller or the buyer to pay compensation to a licensee is not determinative of an agency relationship. The broker's compensation is determined by a brokerage agreement, not by an agency disclosure.

Agency disclosure does not create obligations on the part of the buyer or seller. While the agency disclosure does not place any legal obligations on the seller, the listing contract does obligate the seller to pay a commission. Buyers may be obligated to work exclusively with one agent, depending on the type of buyer agency agreement: exclusive or nonexclusive.

The agency disclosure is an acknowledgment that the broker's form of agency has been discussed with the consumer. Later, the consumer signs an agency document as proof that the licensee discussed the various agency options. What is critical to understand is that once accepted, this disclosure imposes obligations on the role of the licensee/agent. Specific assistance can be entertained any time once meaningful discussion of agency has taken place. Written approval may be obtained at this time, but it is not required until the client actually writes an offer or signs a listing.

Failure to discuss agency in writing prior to the consumer entering a transaction is evidence of a violation under the Iowa Code, Section 543B.34, Subsection 4. However, failure to disclose agency does not affect the validity of title to real property already transferred.

Unless a written notice to the contrary exists, licensees are prohibited from accepting undisclosed compensation (related to a transaction) from any person other than the agreed parties. Licensees also must disclose in writing when acting in a transaction on their own behalf, on behalf of an immediate family member or brokerage, or on behalf of a business entity in which the licensee has an interest.

Brokerage agreements are essentially employment contracts that discuss the duties and responsibilities of the parties. Brokers enter into employment agreements with their affiliated licensees, with sellers, with buyers, with landlords, and with tenants. Brokerage agreements confirm compensation issues.

Brokerage is defined as the business or occupation of a real estate broker. A real estate broker is defined as a person licensed to buy, sell, exchange, or lease real property for others and to charge a fee for those services. Thus a licensed real estate broker engages in the business of brokerage.

Iowa requires a person to have an active real estate license in order to act as an agent, to advertise services as an agent, to negotiate, to collect rents, or to procure prospects for real estate–related activities. Also, by definition, a broker may prepare offers to purchase, listing contracts, agency disclosures, real property residential and agricultural rental agreements, real property commercial rental agreements on one year or less, and groundwater hazard statements, including any addendums, modifications, or amendments to these specific documents. Brokers may not charge for preparation of the legal documents authorized by the court rule.

Brokerage Agreements Between Brokers And Clients Brokerage agreements are contracts between brokers and clients that establish the relationship between the parties as to the brokerage services to be performed and contain the required duties brokers must perform under Iowa Code. These agreements are entered into by the
brokerage with sellers, buyers, tenants, and landlords. The rules are the same whether the real estate is residential, commercial, industrial, or special purpose.

Brokerage agreements may take several forms. A seller hires a broker under a listing agreement. An agreement between a broker and a buyer is a buyer brokerage agreement. A management agreement is a contract between an owner of rental property and the broker who is hired to manage that property.

Even if an affiliate salesperson or associate broker negotiates the agreement, the contract is still between the consumer and the broker. It is important to remember that the agency disclosure merely acknowledges disclosure; the aforementioned brokerage agreements address exclusivity and compensation issues.

Legal and ethical implications of agency and certain duties of loyalty (confidentiality) may survive even after the termination of a brokerage agreement. Examples include accounting for monies and property related to and received during the contractual period, as well as keeping confidentially requested information confidential.

Legal Requirements For Buyer Brokerage Agreements To be legally enforceable, all buyer-brokerage agreements must be in writing and contain statements disclosing the brokerage policy (if any) on cooperating with and compensating other brokerages. Additionally, duties and responsibilities of the buyer/client and the broker/agent should be spelled out. The buyer's agent is not responsible for conducting a property inspection. Compensation issues should be addressed.

The Iowa Supreme Court makes it mandatory that licensees receive written permission in order to prepare real estate–related forms on the buyer's behalf. This written condition must become a part of the agreement.

Iowa rules do not specifically address additional terms of a buyer brokerage agreement. However, by considering the requirements for a listing agreement with a seller, it would appear that the buyer's brokerage agreement should include the broker's authority to assist the buyer in locating, for purchase, lease, or other acquisition, real property identified during the term of the agreement. Compensation and cooperation with other brokers should be addressed.

Besides this buyer-client, other potential buyers that the agent is working with may be interested in the same property. The brokerage agency agreement terms should clarify how the buyer's agent may also represent those other buyers as well, regardless whether the situation arises before, during, or after the end of the contract. Again, in looking at the requirement for preserving confidentiality with sellers, under the buyer brokerage agreement, the licensee should not disclose to either buyer the terms of the other's offer. The agreement should discuss methods of contacting competing buyers.

Also in the terms of the agreement, the broker should ask the buyer to acknowledge that the licensee is solely acting as an agent and not as an attorney, a tax advisor, a lender, an appraiser, a surveyor, a structural engineer, a property inspector, a consultant, or any other professional advisor. Buyers are advised to seek professional advice concerning the condition of the property, the status of the title, and other legal and tax matters concerning any proposed transaction.
Minimum Services
Iowa law (543B.56A Brokerage Agreements Contents) requires brokerage agreements to include four specific requirements known as minimum services. These are as follows:

1. Agents will accept delivery of and present to the client offers and counteroffers to buy, sell, rent, lease, or exchange the client's property or the property the client seeks to purchase or lease. 2. Agents will assist the client in the development, communication, negotiation, and presentation of offers or counteroffers until a rental agreement, lease, exchange agreement, offer to buy or sell, or purchase agreement is signed and all contingencies are satisfied or waived and the transaction is completed. 3. Agents will answer client questions relating to the brokerage agreements, listing agreements, offers, counteroffers, notices, and contingencies. 4. Agents will provide prospective buyers with access to listed properties.

The broker enters into employment agreements with the licensees who work for the broker. Such agreements permit the licensees to act as agents for the broker. Thus, even though a salesperson or an associate broker may negotiate a listing or a buyer brokerage agreement, the agreement is in the name of the broker.

A broker is responsible for supervising the real estate activities performed by a salesperson or a broker associate employed by or otherwise associated with the broker as the broker's representative, even if the affiliate's license is classified as independent contractor. The salesperson or the associate broker is responsible for keeping the employing broker fully informed of all activities conducted on the broker's behalf and any other activities that might affect the broker's responsibilities.

In Iowa, the broker who fails to properly supervise the activities of a salesperson or a broker associate is subject to a civil penalty of $2,500. The broker is still responsible for the associate's activities, even if the associate does not keep the broker fully informed.
Unless the broker was not properly supervising the agent, the broker is not held responsible for an affiliate licensee's actions if the broker had no guilty knowledge of the licensee's actions.

Procuring cause in a real estate transaction means that a licensee started or caused a chain of events that resulted in the sale of a listed property. Procuring cause disputes happen between cooperative brokers and are normally settled by arbitration through local real estate boards or associations. The IREC specifically does not have jurisdiction over disputes between brokers as to fees and commissions.

Any commission or fee in any brokerage agreement is fully negotiable among the parties to that brokerage agreement. The listing contract must spell out the broker's commission rate. It can be either a percentage of the sale or a flat fee.

Once the parties to a brokerage agreement agree on the structure of the commission, no party other than the listing agent is allowed to alter or attempt to alter the commission arrangement without the prior written consent of both the seller and listing agent. Moreover, without the listing agent's prior written consent, Iowa licensees are not allowed to induce buyers to write contracts that seek to alter commission arrangements. The seller, in the listing contract, may authorize the listing company to share compensation with other licensees, including a buyer's agent who solely represents the buyer.

A property management agreement (or property management contract) is between the brokerage and the property owner who wishes to lease real property but does not want to deal directly with tenants and the property. The owner hires a real estate licensee to manage the property—that is, locate tenants, handle repairs, collect rents, and so forth. Iowa rules require this contract for a broker's services to be in writing.

In Iowa, if a licensee wants to become a property owner's authorized leasing agent, a current written property management agreement is required to be on file with the licensee's broker. Written property management agreements or comparable written authorizations signed by the owner or the owner's authorized agent are required before any brokerage is allowed to represent the owner of the property.

The management agreement must define the structure of the property manager and owner relationship, their specific responsibilities and liabilities, the scope of the manager's authority, fees, and the duration of the management agreement. Generally, the broker is a general agent.
Management Agreement Requirements

Every property management agreement must include a proper identification of the property, all the terms and conditions under which the property is to be managed, and the powers and authority given to the broker by the owner. The terms and conditions stipulating how and when the broker is to remit property income and when periodic written statements of property income and expense are to be forwarded for owner review must also be included.
Additionally, requirements include the following:

i: Authorization for payments to third parties
Broker's compensations for services rendered
Required dollar amounts for security deposits
An effective date of the agreement
Terms and conditions for termination of the property management agreement
Signatures of the broker and owner or authorized representative

b.x: The broker is required to deposit all funds received on behalf of the owner into the broker's trust account, no later than five banking days after the last signature is obtained on a purchase agreement. Collected management fees must be withdrawn from the owner's account at least once a month and deposited into the broker's business operating account. Just remember, the broker must always create a paper trail.

A listing agreement is a contract between an owner (the client) and a real estate broker (the agent) by which the broker is employed as agent of the owner to find a buyer for the owner's real estate. When the seller agrees to terms with the buyer, the owner contract requires the owner to pay the broker a commission.

To have legal recognition, all listing contracts in Iowa must be written. The listing agreement must properly identify the property and the terms and conditions under which the property is to be sold. Specifically, the listing agreement must include the listing price, the commission to be paid, the signatures of all concerned parties, and a definite expiration date. Iowa law specifically prohibits automatic renewal clauses in listing contracts. Agents are required to give a legible
copy of the agreement to the owner as soon as reasonably practical after the listing agreement has been signed by the owner(s).

The agreement should also address any reserved items and, if agreed on, an extender clause (also known as a safety clause or a protection clause). In addition, permission must be given for the installation of a lockbox for purposes of ingress and egress, and permission must be obtained to place a For Sale or For Rent sign. Authorization is required if the listing is going to be shared through a multiple listing service.

To have a valid listing agreement, everyone who has an ownership interest should sign the listing agreement. Discovering ownership can take some work. In rural Iowa, the use of rural directories is essential for locating both agricultural property and those who have legal title to that property.

In rural Iowa, ownership is varied. A corporation, a partnership, or a sole proprietor can own agricultural land. The owner's name as well as the Latin identification of no-named owners sometimes identifies the farm's ownership. Behind an owner's name, Latin words are used to expand the field of ownership. Et al. means "and others"; et vir. means "and husband"; and et ux. means "and wife." Agents in Iowa must be familiar with these phrases.

Exclusive-right-to-sell listing agreements give brokerage firms the exclusive right to market the seller's property during the term of the listing and receive a commission, regardless of which person sells it, including the owner. A variation is the exclusive-agency listing, in which the owner of the property promises to compensate a broker for locating a buyer, but the owner reserves the right to produce the buyer without paying the broker a commission. Iowa rules
state that the listing agreement must clearly state whether the agreement is an exclusive agency or an exclusive-right-to-sell agency.

A protection clause protects the broker from unscrupulous sellers or buyers who take the broker's generated leads and then buy or sell the property after the listing agreement expires to avoid paying a commission to the broker. A protection clause can be included in either the listing or the buyer brokerage agreement and extends beyond the expiration of the agreement. To be enforceable, the agreement must include the protection clause as part of the original agreement and must set a definite protection period.

For listings, before the expiration of the listing agreement, the broker must furnish in writing to the owner the names and addresses of the persons to whom the property was presented during the active term of the listing and for whom protection is sought. Delivery must be by personal service with written receipt, or by both regular and certified mail, return receipt requested. If the seller enters into a contract to sell the property to one of these buyers during the protected period, the seller owes the broker a commission.

While the use of protection clauses in a buyer brokerage agreement is not specifically addressed in Iowa law, if the buyer's broker does include such a clause, it is presumed that the clause would have to be part of the original agreement and mirror the protection clause requirements required in the listing agreement. The clause would have to include a definite protection time frame and state that at the expiration of the agreement, if the buyer purchases, leases, or acquires any interest in any previously shown property by the licensee, the buyer agrees to pay an agreed-on fee. Before the expiration of the agreement, the licensee would have to provide the buyer with a list of the sellers' names and addresses and the property addresses for which protection is sought.

Typically the brokerage agreement terminates and a broker has earned a fee when the buyer and the seller enter into a contract. However, Iowa rules require that the relationship continue until the closing of the transaction or any date of expiration agreed on by the parties.
Iowa Code prohibits licensees from certain brokerage practices that may harm the public. Some practices may also be unethical to other licensees and complicate real estate transactions.
Presenting Offers

Listing agents must allow buyers' agents to accompany their clients at any step in a real estate transaction, except that a listing agent is not required to permit a buyer's agent to be present when presenting an offer to a seller-client or discussing confidential matters with the seller-client. With the listing agent present, buyer's agents are sometimes afforded the courtesy to personally present their client's purchase agreement directly to the seller. If this courtesy is not extended, the buyer's agent must present the buyer's purchase agreement to the listing agent, after which the listing agent (alone) presents the offer to the seller.

When the listing agent presents another agent's offer, then immediately upon receiving the signed and dated offer with consideration, the listing agent must provide a copy of the offer back to the buyer or buyer's agent as a receipt. By following this rule, buyers are afforded the assurance that their offer won't be altered.
Broker Cooperation and Compensation

While cooperation is often a membership requirement, compensation is not required by either license law or the National Association of REALTORS® Code of Ethics. Article 3 of the Code reads, "REALTORS® shall cooperate with other brokers except when cooperation is not in the client's best interest. The obligation to cooperate does not include the obligation to share commissions, fees, or to otherwise compensate another broker."

Brokers recognize that while one brokerage has the listing, another broker may already be working with buyers who want to continue working with their own agent. In this situation, the seller benefits if the listing broker's agreement states willingness to share the compensation with any other broker who procures a buyer.

This cooperation benefits the seller by opening the property to more potential buyers. As noted, Iowa law does not require a broker to either cooperate or compensate other brokers. However, the listing agreement must include a statement disclosing the brokerage policy on cooperating with and compensating other brokerages. This disclosure is intended to inform the client of any policy that might limit the participation of any other brokerage.
Agreements to split the commission between brokers should always appear on separate documents and not on the purchase offer, which is an agreement between a buyer and a seller.

secs.h: When To Place For Sale Signs

b.x: It is illegal to place a sign on any property offering it for sale, rent, or lease without the owner's consent. Thus, the broker may place the sign whenever the seller agrees. Many brokerages include specific authorization for a For Sale or For Rent sign as part of the listing agreement.

Every year, real estate agents help thousands of families by referring them to other licensees across the United States. In return for the referral, a percentage or other agreed-upon fee is paid to the referring broker. These fees are legal if paid between brokers.
Two prohibited referral practices address contractual interference:

i: A licensee is not allowed to request a referral fee for a buyer who has already made a bona fide offer, accepted by a seller.
A licensee is not allowed to request a referral fee for a seller who has already signed a bona fide listing agreement.

b.x: Also, it is unlawful for licensees to pay referral or finder fees to unlicensed third parties for procuring prospects or engaging in any activity that requires a real estate license.

A net listing is an agreement that specifies a net sale price to be received by the owner with the excess over that price to be received by the broker as commission. This situation presents a potential conflict of interest for the broker.

Often, the seller only realizes the true selling price of the property when an offer to purchase is obtained. Because of the appearance of conflict between the fiduciary broker-client relationship and the broker's profit motive, the taking of a net listing is considered unprofessional conduct and constitutes a violation of the Iowa Code.

Legally binding listing agreements must be respected by outside parties. Alienating those involved in contractual relationships is illegal. According to Iowa license law, licensees are not allowed to negotiate or enter into listing agreements if it is known that the owner has an existing written, unexpired exclusive-right-to-sell listing agreement. Simply stated, agents are not allowed to solicit listings with another brokerage that have not been terminated.

However, from time to time, a seller who is under contract with a broker may contact a second broker and want to discuss listing with the second broker. The second broker may talk with a seller who initiates the call. However, the second broker cannot ethically discuss the existing broker's marketing strategies or techniques or make disparaging remarks about the first broker. Also, any listing entered into cannot become effective until the first listing is either canceled or expires.

Listing agreements may not be assigned, sold, or otherwise transferred to another broker without the express written consent of all the parties to the original agreement. On termination, licensees are not allowed to take or use any written listing agreements secured during their employment.
Brokerage agreements are the property of the principal broker and can be canceled only by the broker and the seller, unless the terms of the contract state otherwise.
Transferring Buyer Brokerage Agreements To Another Broker

Unless the terms of the agreement state otherwise, buyer brokerage contracts cannot be assigned, sold, or otherwise transferred to another broker without the express written consent of all parties to the original agreement.

On termination, licensees are not allowed to take or use any written buyer brokerage agreements secured during their employment. These agreements remain the property of the principal broker and may be canceled only by the broker and the buyer client.

t: Iowa Contracts, Required Forms and Closing
