b.x: This unit covers general information on contracts, including requirements for creating contracts, rules for offers and acceptances, and required forms for real estate transactions. Closing concerns including abstracting, declaration of value, and conveyance taxes are also covered. This unit also discusses required disclosures associated with the Groundwater Hazard
Statement, the Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement, stigmatized properties, and environmental topics.

Real estate licensees deal with contracts in every area of the real estate business. Listing agreements, sales agreements, leases, property management agreements, and buyer brokerage agreements are just some of the contracts used daily in real estate.
Contract

A contract is a set of legally binding promises between two informed parties that must be performed and for which, if a breach occurs, the law provides a remedy. To be legally enforceable, everything related to the transfer of Iowa real estate must be in writing.

In Iowa, upon execution of any instrument in connection with a real estate transaction, licensees are required as soon as practical to deliver legible copies of the original document to each party. It is the responsibility of the licensee to prepare sufficient copies of such instruments to satisfy this requirement.
Informed Parties

Before entering into a legally binding contract to buy or sell real estate, what the parties must offer and accept must be the same. Hence, it is important that sellers disclose every important issue about the property. Otherwise, the buyer is buying less than agreed on. It is an act of fraud to withhold disclosure of material adverse facts. Sometimes, a seller or an agent does not know, or negligently withholds, information. In these situations, the buyer may be able to void the contract.
Material Adverse Fact

In Iowa, material adverse facts are those conditions or occurrences that are generally recognized as being of such significance that they would affect either party's decision to enter into a contract. Included in this definition are situations that

i: significantly and adversely affect the value of a property,
significantly reduce the structural integrity of a property, and
present a significant health risk to the occupants of the property.

b.x: Fraudulent Acts

Fraudulent acts require intentional deception in such a way as to harm another person. Included in this definition are fraudulent advertising, making false statements about a property's condition, and intentionally concealing known facts. Such fraudulent acts are subject to license suspension or revocation.
Negligence

Misrepresentation or omission of pertinent facts does not have to be intentional to bring liability exposure. Negligent misrepresentation occurs when licensees should have known that incorrect statements were being relied on as material fact.

Only attorneys are permitted to prepare contracts. However, incidental to residential transactions, the Iowa Supreme Court requires that real estate brokerage companies obtain written authorization from clients and customers in order to complete purchase agreements, addendums, amendments, groundwater hazard statements, and declarations of value documents. Because these are legally binding documents, consumers are encouraged to seek competent legal advice before signing.

In other words, with written permission and at the direction of the client or customer, a real estate licensee can assist the transaction by filling in the blanks of attorney-prepared forms. For those contractual documents over which the broker has control, failure to obtain all signatures or
initials of the required parties is subject to disciplinary action and a civil penalty. The licensee must deliver signed copies to all parties as soon as possible.
What Brokers May Not Prepare

In Iowa, real estate brokers should be cautious to avoid the charge of practicing law without a license. Brokers are not allowed to prepare deeds, affidavits of child support or spousal support, or installment sales contracts or documents necessary to correct title defects. Licensed attorneys must be used to prepare these documents.

Iowa is an agricultural state and, as such, it has large tracts of farm ground. Rectangular survey is a common form of measurement in rural Iowa, while metes-and-bounds descriptions are often used in municipal areas. The measurements are surveyed using compass directions and linear feet. Once subdivision proposals are submitted for approval and recorded, plats are then adopted for future legal descriptions.

There must be a meeting of the minds to make a contract, and a street address is not definitive enough to clarify what is being purchased. Because of their temporary nature, street addresses are not considered legal descriptions. To be lawful, one must be able to use a legal description to walk its boundaries. A street address may be sufficient in a listing agreement, but it is best that the legal description appear in an offer to purchase to be sure of a legally binding contract.

Required Forms For Real Estate Transactions In addition to the purchase agreement, Iowa requires the use of three forms: Agency Disclosure, Groundwater Hazard Statement, and a Declaration of Value. The sale of

residential properties requires another form or two: the Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement with a separate signature requirement for radon and a radon brochure for distribution; and, if the residence was built prior to 1978, a lead-based-paint disclosure form and booklet.

Iowa Commission rules require that every broker deliver a complete detailed closing statement to the seller and, at the same time, a detailed closing statement to the buyer. These are often called "in and out" files. The broker must retain copies of these closing statements for five years after the date of closing, along with a copy of the listing, any offers to purchase, and all pertinent correspondence.

When preparing to enter into contracts for the sale or rental of real property, buyers, sellers, and tenants want to make decisions based on full knowledge of the property and the title. Additionally, in today's marketplace, the real estate industry has seen a movement from caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) to seller disclose. Today, sellers are asked to disclose information material to a buyer making an informed decision.

The Iowa Real Estate Commission (IREC) has addressed these concerns. and requires various written disclosures including the Groundwater Hazard Statement, the Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement, and radon and lead-based paint disclosures.

Iowa's Groundwater Hazard Statement (DNR Form 543-0960) is required in the transfer of any real property in Iowa. It requires that the transferor (or agent) disclose to the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) information about the location of any wells, active or abandoned, on the transferred property. Information is also requested about the known presence of any
solid-waste disposal system, the storage of any known hazardous wastes, the presence of any underground storage tanks, and any private burial sites with one or more graves containing human remains.

In order to complete the Groundwater Hazard Statement, a state-certified inspector must approve the existing septic system. A few exemptions exist: foreclosure, testate and intestate transfers, transfers between joint tenants or tenants in common, transfers between spouses and family members, and transfers with the intent to demolish.
The recorder of deeds will not record a deed unless this statement accompanies the deed. Failure to provide this statement does not affect the transfer of the property.

Iowa's Declaration of Value form is required by the Department of Revenue and Financing to declare the total amount paid, the financial details if it is an individual contract sale, and a checklist of all the sales conditions applicable to the sale. Because the form is shared with the county assessor, it is imperative that the sales conditions germane to the sale be disclosed. The assessor needs to know the sales conditions to determine whether the property was sold at or below market value The form may be completed by the seller, the buyer, or the agent for either one. Certain transfers are exempt. If the form is not correctly filled out, the county recorder is required by law to refuse to record the contract, deed, or other instrument conveying the affected property. Visit www.iowa.gov/tax/forms/propdov.html.
Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement (1 of 4)

The purpose of the Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement is to forewarn prospective buyers of all known conditions materially affecting the property before writing an offer. If the procedures are not followed, the buyer can revoke the offer.

The disclosure statement includes information about the property's plumbing, electrical, and heating systems; any significant structural defects; presence of pests; amount of any special assessments; and zoning classification. The Commission provides sample language for the disclosure in Rule 1.39(6). However, no particular language is required in the disclosure statement as long as the required disclosure items are included.

Both the seller and the buyer must acknowledge with their signatures the delivery/receipt of the Iowa Radon Home-Buyers and Sellers Fact Sheet as prepared by the Iowa Department of Health. The fact sheet may be obtained from http://www.eiowainspections.com/reports/radon.pdf.
Timing of the Property Disclosure

The disclosure statement is to be delivered to the buyer by personal delivery or by certified/registered mail. It must be delivered before the transferor either makes a written offer to sell or accepts a written offer for the transfer of the real property.

To comply with the law, only delivery is required before a seller accepts an offer. The rules say that the agent should attempt to obtain the buyer's signature. If the disclosure is not timely made, then the transferee may withdraw the offer or revoke the acceptance without liability within three days following personal delivery of the statement or five days following delivery by mail.
Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement (2 of 4) Properties Requiring the Seller Property Disclosure and Exemptions

Iowa's Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement is required if the property has at least one but not more than four dwelling units. It does not apply to transfers of commercial and industrial properties of five or more residential units. Even for residential units, there are certain exemptions.
Some property owners and/or transactions are exempt by law. Exempt transactions include the following:

i: A transfer made by court order, including an execution of a judgment, foreclosure of a mortgage, forfeiture of a real estate contract, transfer by a trustee in bankruptcy, transfer by eminent domain, or transfer for specific performance
A transfer to or from the state, a political subdivision of the state, another state, or the United States
An executor or administrator (a fiduciary) of a decedent's estate
A transfer between joint tenants or tenants in common
A transfer between spouses or a transfer resulting from a divorce decree
A transfer to a spouse or a person in the lineal line of consanguinity (blood relative)
A transfer by quitclaim deed

b.x: Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement (3 of 4)
Who Must Make the Property Disclosure

The disclosure statement applies to any owner interested in transferring real property or a broker or salesperson acting on behalf of the owner. The owner is required to deliver a written disclosure statement to any person interested in receiving the real property. Under Iowa Code, Chapter 14, Section 193E.14.1(6), the disclosure statement can satisfy the Iowa radon fact sheet requirement when it includes both of the following statements:

i: Seller acknowledges requirement that buyer(s) be provided with the Iowa Radon Home-Buyers and Sellers Fact Sheet, prepared by the Iowa Department of Public Health.
Buyer(s) acknowledges receipt of the Iowa Radon Home-Buyers and Sellers Fact Sheet, prepared by the Iowa Department of Public Health.

b.x: Consequences if the Disclosure Is Not Made or Made After the Offer Has Been Accepted

If the seller or the seller's agent does not deliver the disclosure statement in a timely manner, a buyer may withdraw an offer or revoke its acceptance without liability within three days following personal delivery of the statement or five days if delivered by mail. If it is not delivered before closing, the seller may be liable for damages.
A transfer is not invalidated solely because of a failure of a person to comply with the written disclosure requirement.
How Changes Should Be Handled After the Seller Filled Out the Property Disclosure Form

Once delivered, any new discoveries (e.g., previous termite infestation) require an amended statement. Once the owner or the owner's agent has knowledge of any previously unknown defects, that information must be communicated to the buyer. Unless otherwise amended, any inaccurate or misleading information on the original disclosure is assumed to be accurate and complete, and failure to disclose any subsequently known defects is considered fraud.
Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement (4 of 4) Licensee's Responsibilities

In Iowa, the listing agent is required to obtain a completed disclosure signed and dated by each seller represented by the brokerage. Then the licensee makes sure that the executed statement is delivered to either the potential buyer or the buyer's agent before any offer is written. The listing agent then requests a signed and dated copy of the form before any offer is presented to the seller.

Real estate licensees are not liable for the error, inaccuracy, or omission in information required in a disclosure statement unless the licensee has actual knowledge of the accuracy, or fails to exercise ordinary care in obtaining the information.

The buyer's agent is responsible for informing the buyer that the seller is obligated to deliver the property disclosure statement and that, without the buyer's signature and date, the sale may be negated based on the "without liability" rule. If, within three days following the late personal delivery of the statement or five days following any late delivery by mail, the disclosure statement is not timely delivered, the buyer may withdraw the offer or revoke an already accepted offer "without liability."
If a transaction closes, the listing broker must maintain the completed disclosure statement for a minimum of five years.
Required Signatures on the Seller Property Disclosure Form

Commission rules require that, at the time of the listing, the licensee obtain a completed disclosure signed and dated by each seller. When the disclosure is delivered to the buyer, the licensee should at least attempt to obtain the buyer's signature and date of signature.

Sellers disclose that the provided information regarding the property's condition is based on information known or reasonably available to them and certify that the information is true and accurate to the best of their knowledge. Buyers acknowledge receipt of the document but note that the document is not intended to be a warranty or a substitute for any inspection deemed necessary by the buyers. If there is more than one buyer, any one buyer may accept delivery of the executed statement.
If unable to obtain the buyer's signature, the licensee must obtain other documentation establishing delivery of the disclosure.

Iowa operates under the federal Title X Lead-Based Paint Poisoning Prevention Act passed in 1992 and the Iowa Residential Lead-Based Paint Disclosure Program-Section 1018 of Title 10. This legislation requires notification of the possible exposure of lead-based paint in all pre-1978 residential and apartment dwellings. The Iowa Department of Public Health is the authority on lead-based-paint issues. In Iowa, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has jurisdiction over lead-based-paint disclosure enforcement.

The seller is required to notify the buyer of any known lead-based hazards and provide the buyer with any information on lead-based hazards from risk assessments or inspections in the seller's possession. The seller must also provide a booklet to the buyer or the tenant. Buyers (but not tenants) have the right to have the property inspected within ten days or any period agreed on or to waive this right. Failure to disclose any known presence is subject to a $10,000 fine per violation. Copies of these disclosures must be retained for three years.

Licensees must be careful in handling the process of offer and acceptance to avoid potential misunderstandings among the parties to a real estate transaction or legal issues for licensees. Licensees must also be knowledgeable of the closing process, including their responsibilities under Iowa law. Iowa assesses a tax on the transfer of real estate, which must be paid when the deed is recorded.

Listing agents are not required to permit a buyer's agent to be present when presenting offers or discussing confidential matters with their seller clients. However, in some Iowa brokerage communities, it is customary to give buyer's agents the privilege of presenting their buyer's offer.
Presenting Multiple Offers

The IREC rule states that any and all offers received by a listing agent must be promptly presented to the seller for consideration or the listing broker may face disciplinary action. Sellers must be permitted to view all offers to determine which offer is best for them. The formal acceptance or rejection must then be promptly communicated to the prospective buyer or the buyer's agent.

Licensees need to help the buyer understand that another offer may be presented while the seller is considering the first offer. No particular courtesies are extended to the person writing the first offer. There is no particular advantage to writing the first offer.

Sometimes other offers arrive after the seller accepts an offer. The seller has the right to see offers that arrive even after the seller has accepted an offer. The seller is still bound to the accepted offer, but may wish to view a later offer as a possible backup or secondary offer.

Once the offer is accepted, the buyer has certain rights in the property. After a purchase agreement is signed and the buyer or the buyer's agent is in possession of the signed document, equitable title passes to the purchaser. At this point, the buyer has an insurable interest in the property and is allowed the opportunity to purchase additional insurance. The seller cannot arbitrarily withdraw acceptance and sell to another party.

Dual contracts are illegal in Iowa. The term dual contracts refers to two contracts from the same buyer on the same property. One of the offers is used to purchase the property while the other is used to finance the property. The offer to purchase can be either written or just an oral arrangement, while the offer to finance is generally written.

The true purchase price is known only between the contracting parties. The purpose of these contracts is to enable the buyer to obtain a larger loan than the true sale price or to enable the buyer to qualify for a loan that the buyer otherwise could not obtain. Thus, the lender is
deceived. In Iowa, any person who violates this law is guilty of a fraudulent practice and is subject to disciplinary action.

Closing Responsibilities And Practices (1 of 3) The buyer can request that some funds be withheld from the seller until all repairs are completed. In the event all trust funds cannot be disbursed at closing, the broker is required to obtain an escrow agreement signed by both parties that directs the broker regarding the future disbursement of the escrowed funds. Funds are retained in a trust account.
Even though the task may be delegated to another entity, the listing broker is responsible for the closing. Therefore, Iowa law authorizes the listing company to coordinate the closing.
Closing Responsibilities And Practices (2 of 3) Responsibility for Retaining Copies of All Closing Documents
At closing, the broker is required to keep copies of all executed documents for five years.

The seller's closing statement shows all the receipts and disbursements handled by the broker. The buyer's closing statement shows all monies received by the broker and how and for what they were disbursed. These documents are prepared by the closing broker and retained for at least five years after the date of closing. Included in this list of documents are

i: voided offers,
voided checks,
records,
contracts,
closing statements,
disclosure documents like agency and lead-based paint,
signed documents, and
related correspondence to the transaction.

b.x: According to the Iowa Supreme Court ruling in 2001, real estate brokers cannot charge a fee for the preparation of purchase agreements, groundwater hazard statements, or declaration of value documents.
Closing Responsibilities And Practices (3 of 3) Lien-Theory State

Iowa is a lien-theory state. This means that, instead of a deed, the owner-borrower gives the lender a mortgage lien to use as collateral. The lender has the owner-borrower sign a promissory note as evidence of the debt and sign a mortgage lien instrument as collateral for the debt. If the owner defaults on the loan, the lender can file for a judicial foreclosure on the property. In Iowa, the owner-borrower never relinquishes legal title.
Good and Marketable Title

Buyers need to know that title to the property is good and marketable. Iowa is an abstract state. An abstractor examines the recorded history of the property, and then this report is given to the buyer's attorney for an opinion. Title defects discovered by the examination may then be corrected.

Once the buyer's attorney is satisfied that marketable title can be transferred, the lender proceeds with the closing. The deed is delivered, and legal title passes to the purchaser. Customarily, deeds are recorded before the financing company releases the borrower's funds.
Responsibility for Searching Public Records

The owner of the property is usually required to promptly provide an abstract of title continuation and convey it to the buyer's attorney for an opinion about the quality of title. Sellers are required to make every reasonable effort to promptly perfect the title in accordance with the opinion so that on conveyance, title is deemed marketable in compliance with the purchase agreement and the land title laws of the state of Iowa.

If closing is delayed due to the seller's inability to provide marketable title, both parties may work toward closing or give each other written notice that the contract is to be rescinded. Sellers are not allowed to rescind unless they have made every reasonable attempt to produce marketable title.

Iowa charges property owners a transfer tax when they transfer legal title to their properties. Historically, Iowa used differing denomination stamps (postage-stamp size) to record the amount of the tax and affixed them to the deed. The stamps were then franked (defaced) to show that the tax had been paid. To the property owner, it was considered a transfer tax stamp. To the State of Iowa, it was considered a revenue stamp. To the recorder's office, it was considered a documentary stamp. In reality, it was the same thing looked at from three perspectives.

Today, Iowa uses either a receipt or a bar code and affixes it to the deed for recordation. However, it is still called a revenue stamp, but it is not; it's just a revenue tax. Seewww.iowa.gov/tax/taxlaw/taxtypes.html#real.
Computing Conveyance Taxes

As of 2011, the transfer tax is 80 cents per $500.00, or $1.60 per thousand, the first $500.00 being exempt. The formula to determine the revenue tax is: 1) always reduce the selling price to the next increment of $500.00; then 2) multiply the remaining number of thousands by $1.60.
For example, here is how to compute the taxes on a $300,000 sale:
Step 1. $300,000 reduced to the nearest increment of $500 is $299,500.
Step 2. (299,500/1,000)= 299.5 × $1.60 = a transfer tax or revenue tax of $479.20.

Typically, at closing, this amount is paid out of the seller's proceeds to the state of Iowa. The tax is payable when the deed or other instrument conveying the real property is presented for recording.

It is important for licensees to be aware of local environmental issues, environmental state laws, and enforcement agencies, and to practice proper disclosure. Licensees are expected to help their clients locate information about hazardous substances. Also, licensees should understand their responsibilities in dealing with stigmatized property.

The state agency that controls water rights in Iowa is the Iowa Department of Natural Resources (DNR). Chapter 455B of the Iowa Code establishes the jurisdiction of water-related concerns with the DNR. For reference, Part 4 of the Code, 455B.261-282, deals with water allocation and use and floodplain control.

Two large rivers border Iowa, the Mississippi River to the east and the Missouri River to the west. Iowa law allows all owners or lessees of land situated on the Iowa banks of either river to construct and maintain piers, cribs, and booms in front of their property. Owners may also construct and maintain any other proper and convenient erections and devices for their respective pursuits and the protection and harbor for rafts, logs, floats, and watercraft in such a manner as to create no material or unreasonable obstruction to the navigational commerce of the rivers.
Permission to divert, store, or withdraw water must be cleared with the Iowa DNR.

A buyer may learn more about wetlands protection from Iowa's Department of Agriculture, Iowa's Farm Service Agency, Iowa's Department of Natural Resources (Wetlands Acquisition, Inventory, Preservation, and Restoration Division), county conservation boards, as well as Iowa State University's county Extension Offices. These organizations serve as consultants on agricultural and wetlands issues.

Iowa passed the Clean Water Act in 1972 and amended the act in 1977 and 1987. Section 404 is the primary federal authority for protecting America's wetlands. Under Section 404, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the EPA have concurrent jurisdictional authority over the dredging and filling of U.S. waters, including wetlands.

The Clean Water Act of 1977 makes it unlawful for any person to discharge any pollutant from a point source into navigable waters unless a permit is obtained from the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES). This means that developers must obtain permits and implement environmentally safe action plans to prevent eroded soil from polluting our waterways.
Wetlands Issues for Developers

Much to the chagrin of developers, rigid wetlands definitions require them to obtain permits for dredging and other activities that remove materials from wetlands. For example, developers who want to maintain storm-water detention ponds that provide water-purifying features and recreational amenities should begin very early in the process to work with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers or face delays because of regulatory barriers.
Other water-related issues are associated with wells and septic systems.

Customarily, well testing is done in Iowa for bacteria and high levels of nitrate. The Residential Property Seller Disclosure Statement should include copies of water tests, if available. The Iowa Department of Public Health is the definitive authority over water quality. The Limnology Division monitors and analyzes water quality in Iowa's lakes, reservoirs, streams, rivers, and wastewater treatment plants.
Abandoned wells are required by Iowa law to be filled within 90 days.

In Iowa, county health officials monitor septic tanks and private sewage disposal systems. Iowa allows the use of both aerobic and anaerobic systems. For proper drainage, the ground must be able to absorb the liquid waste. A percolation test is conducted that monitors the time that it
takes water poured through a pipe to be absorbed by the soil. A permit may not be issued if there is insufficient absorption.

County health standards require anaerobic systems to drain into either laterals or a wetlands ecosystem. It is a violation of county health standards to drain septic tank waste directly into a ditch. Sellers are required to disclose any known septic tank or private sewage system problems on the state-mandated seller's property condition disclosure document. As discussed earlier, in order to complete the Groundwater Hazard Statement required to record a deed, a state-certified inspector must have approved any existing septic system (DNR Form 543-0960).

Responsibility for cleaning up hazardous waste on a property varies. Because cleanups can be quite costly, prospective buyers should certainly obtain as many reports as are available from the EPA, DNR, and even from private environmental specialists. On contaminated sites, Iowa's DNR can require a Site Cleanup Report (SCR) or a Cleanup Action Design Report (CADR). Water contamination is the big issue, and in 1987, Iowa created its own Iowa Groundwater Protection Act.
Implementation of CERCLA in Iowa

Iowa's Department of Natural Resources (DNR), Solid Waste Section, is the enforcement agency for Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act's (CERCLA) Superfund and Uncontrolled Site Regulations in Iowa. CERCLA's Superfund is used to clean up abandoned, leaking hazardous waste sites that threaten public health and contaminate the environment. The worst sites are placed on a National Priority List (NPL), and Iowa has several NPL sites, many of which have been cleaned up or contained. In Iowa, the

lawful discharge of animal manure is not regulated under CERCLA. DNR spells out its authority to deny or modify factory farm construction permits or manure management plans in order to protect Iowa's waterways. Seewww.iowadnr.gov/InsideDNR/RegulatoryWater/WastewaterConstruction/ConstructionPermit s.aspx.
Disclosures of Environmental Presence, such as Asbestos, Radon, Etc.

The Commission specifically recommends that the seller of residential property disclose the presence of asbestos, radon, and lead-based paint. Many brokers have broadened the form to include other environmental issues.
Iowa UST (Underground Storage Tanks) Bill

In 1986, Iowa passed its own UST bill, which required that UST owners retrofit outdated steel tanks with corrosion-protected or fiberglass-lined tanks before January 1, 1995. Also, the UST bill provided an Iowa UST Fund for insurance to assist in the cost of retrofitting. Without the insurance, the UST owner was considered self-insured. Iowa's environmental laws (Sections 455A-455G) are enforced by Iowa's DNR.

A stigmatized property is one that has acquired an undesirable reputation. Stigmatized properties include homes with recorded paranormal activities, those psychologically impacted by newsworthy incidents such as murder or murder/suicide, or those suspected of being a front for illegal drug sales or a site of a forcible felony.
Responsibility for Failure to Disclose Information about Stigmatized Property

The essence of the issue is discovery, not disclosure. There is no duty for the seller to disclose such information. However, if disclosed, an agent must decide how to proceed. An agent may take the listing and not disclose or take the listing and (with permission) disclose to a buyer's agent the events that led up to the decision to list. Ethically, the listing agent would like to obtain permission to disclose the stigma to the buyer's agent just before the buyer's written offer is presented. In this scenario, a buyer who feels uncomfortable with the situation could withdraw the offer.

Based on Iowa court cases, no cause of action is warranted against a buyer's agent for failure to discover that the purchased property was psychologically impacted. However, if the buyer's agent had prior knowledge, then under agency law, the buyer's agent may have a fiduciary duty to disclose the unknown information to the client.

b.x: This unit covers how the Iowa Real Estate Commission (IREC) considers violations of license law or rule. Generally, after proper disciplinary hearings, the IREC exercises its control over licensees through public reprimands, reeducation, fines, and the denial, suspension, or revocation of licenses.

The IREC also requires an added protection to provide compensation to a consumer who suffers monetary damage because of a licensee's error or negligence. Each active licensee is required to purchase errors and omissions (E&O) insurance, which is similar to malpractice insurance.

The IREC may pursue a complaint against a licensee for violations of the license act or against nonlicensees before any court of competent jurisdiction and take any necessary legal actions to enforce the law and collect penalties.

In addition, an injunction may be granted through an action in district court to prohibit a person from engaging in activities that violate licensure requirements. If convicted, the affected person is entitled to actual costs and attorney fees.
The IREC is charged with protecting the interests of the public. Consequently, the Commission has jurisdiction over actions by a licensee that can harm the consumer in a real estate transaction.

The Commission may investigate a licensee's actions for any of the following reasons: fraudulent activities, substantial misrepresentations, undisclosed dual agency, accepting a commission as a licensee from anyone except the brokerage, and representing two brokerages without the knowledge of both brokers.

An investigation may be initiated for other reasons—for example, a broker who fails to account for or remit monies into the broker's trust account in a timely manner, or a broker who pays a bird-dog fee (commission) for real estate referrals to someone who is not licensed. Other reasons include failing to provide requested information to the Commission in a timely manner (within 14 days) or any other conduct that demonstrates deceit or professional incompetence, including habitual intoxication or an addiction to drugs.

Iowa Real Estate Commission's Investigatory Power The IREC is allowed to investigate the actions of any licensee on its own motion and/or on the receipt of a verified written complaint. In connection with an investigation, the Commission is

authorized by Iowa law to subpoena books, papers, records, and even witnesses. The Commission has authority to conduct hearings, and licensees who are found guilty may have their licenses revoked or suspended. Witnesses who fail to cooperate may be found guilty of contempt of court.

Normally, a written complaint is filed; the complaint includes the complainant's full name, address, and telephone number, plus the same information about the respondent. The complainant must include a concise statement of the facts, clearly and accurately apprising the Commission of the allegations against the respondent. The complaint can be either personally delivered or mailed to the executive secretary of the Commission for review.

The executive secretary acts as a gatekeeper. If the evidence indicates a possible violation that falls within the jurisdiction of the Commission, the executive secretary refers the complaint to the Commission's two- to five-member investigating committee. However, if the complaint does not meet certain criteria, the executive secretary has the prerogative to decline to pursue the complaint. If the complaint is declined, the executive secretary informs the complainant by letter with a statement specifying the reasons for rejection.

Reasons To Conclude An Investigation Without A Hearing If the committee determines that no probable cause exists to warrant discipline, a letter is sent and the case is closed. Reasons for refusing to conduct a hearing include the triviality of the allegation, insufficient evidence, effort to solve on a local level, lack of clarity of the issue, and lack of jurisdiction.

Recall that the mission of the Commission is to protect the public. Thus, Commission rules do not authorize the Commission to consider or conduct hearings involving disputes over fees or commissions between cooperating brokers, salespersons, and other brokers.
The investigating committee considers the severity of the violation and the sufficiency of evidence in determining the appropriate hearing process to follow in resolving the complaint.

In determining the appropriate action, the investigating committee considers not only the severity of the violation and the sufficiency of evidence but also the possibility that the problem could be better resolved by other means available to the parties, without Commission involvement. The Commission discusses the clarity of the laws and rules that support the claim of the alleged violation, the clarity of the Commission's jurisdiction, whether the violation is likely to recur, and the record of the licensee.

If the appointed investigating committee determines that a violation warranting disciplinary action has occurred, then a disciplinary case will be opened against the respondent. If necessary, the investigating committee will assign an investigator to obtain additional information.

On completion of its investigation, the Commission may request (not demand) that the licensee and the licensee's employing broker attend an informal, closed-session hearing to negotiate a settlement. If the licensee chooses, a representative attorney may attend the session. If it is determined that a settlement agreement cannot be reached, the committee may proceed with a formal hearing and use the discussed facts from the informal hearing.

A written notice of a Commission-conducted hearing, together with a statement of charges, is sent by certified mail to the licensee's last known business address at least 20 days before the scheduled contested case hearing. The notice of hearing gives the date, time, and place of the hearing and a statement that authorizes the presence of legal counsel and states the Commission's legal and jurisdictional authority. The Commission includes references to applicable statutes and rules along with a brief statement of the matter.

The respondent must acknowledge receipt within ten days of receiving the hearing notice. Also included is a statement requiring that the respondent furnish a list of potential witnesses (with their current addresses) to the executive secretary within ten days before the scheduled hearing date.

It should be noted, too, that any party to any Commission hearing has the right to the attendance of subpoenaed witnesses. These witnesses are entitled to the same fees and mileage allowances as are prescribed by law in judicial proceedings in civil cases. (See 543B.36 Attendance of witnesses and 543B.37 Fees and mileage.)
Written requests from the respondent for a continuance may be considered no less than seven days before the scheduled hearing, except in the case of an unanticipated emergency.
Testimony may be taken before the hearing by deposition, compelling any involved party to appear and depose in the same manner as witnesses compelled to appear and testify in civil cases.

When a majority of the Commission members preside over the reception of the evidence, the Commission's decision is final. The decision can exonerate the licensee or revoke, suspend, or possibly not renew the license. Other disciplinary actions include probation, additional education or training, reexamination, physical or mental examination, issuing a citation and warning, or imposing a civil penalty not to exceed $2,500.

If the respondent does not appear, the hearing will be held without the licensee. The licensee will be bound by the decision as though present. In other words, the licensee loses the right to cross-examine witnesses and to present a defense.
The respondent may appeal the Commission's action by seeking a judicial review through the Iowa Administrative Procedure Act.

The Iowa Real Estate Commission has several options when punishing licensees for violations of the license law. Licensees should understand the consequences whenever a licensee's license is suspended or revoked.

Generally, after proper disciplinary hearings, the Iowa Real Estate Commission exercises its control over licensees through public reprimands, reeducation, fines, and the denial, suspension, or revocation of licenses. Disciplinary actions include probation, additional education or training, reexamination, physical or mental examination, issuing a citation and warning, or imposing a civil penalty not to exceed $2,500.

Most violations under Iowa license law are considered simple misdemeanors. One exception is permitting or participating in the use of dual contracts. In Iowa, if someone is found guilty of using dual contracts, it is considered a fraudulent (felonious) practice.

Immediate Consequences Of Suspended Or Revoked Licenses A suspended or revoked license must be returned to the Commission, and as of the effective date, the right to engage in activities that require a license is terminated. Note, though, that during the penalty period, a licensee whose license has been suspended or revoked is allowed to receive compensation earned before the effective date of the suspension or revocation.

Effect On Licensees If A Brokerage Is Disciplined The revocation of the broker's (brokerage) license automatically places on inactive status all licensees employed by the broker. These licensees may return to real estate activities only when hired by another designated broker.

Effect On Designated Broker If Licensees Are Disciplined Any unlawful act or violation by a licensee is not cause for the revocation of the broker's license unless the broker had guilty knowledge of the unlawful act or Commission violation. Note, though, that during the penalty period, a licensee whose license has been suspended or revoked is allowed to receive compensation earned prior to the effective date of the suspension or revocation.

b.x: On receipt of the Commission's order, the suspended or revoked broker must cancel all listings and property management agreements. Sellers or lessors must be apprised of their right to list or lease with someone else. It is illegal to sell or assign listings or management agreements without written authorization of the seller or the lessor.

A broker whose license has been suspended or revoked may not finalize any pending closings. With written approval of the concerned parties, this task must be delegated to a new entity that will handle the trust funds and close the transaction. Such entities can include another broker, an attorney, a financial institution, or an escrow company.

All advertising must be canceled within ten days. Brokers whose licenses have been suspended or revoked are also prohibited from advertising real estate in any manner as brokers or answering their business telephones in any manner that might indicate that the brokerage is active in the real estate business.
Iowa does not have a state recovery fund. However, mandatory errors and omissions insurance substitutes for injured party recovery funds.
Iowa Legal Requirements For Bonding And Insurance Iowa law does not require that licensees be bonded. Instead, it requires errors and omissions (E&O) insurance.

Errors And Omissions Insurance Requirements In Iowa E&O insurance is a type of coverage that protects brokers and affiliated licensees from loss due to errors, mistakes, and negligence. Iowa law requires that all active licensees carry E&O insurance. Licensees must annually submit evidence of compliance. If the E&O coverage lapses, the Commission is authorized to place licensees on inactive status and may charge a reinstatement fee.

The Commission requires receipt of proof of E&O insurance from new licensees before the license is issued and before reinstating an expired license if the license has been inactive for more than 20 days. When applying for a real estate license, the applicant must provide proof of E&O coverage or the application will not be approved. Not carrying E&O insurance and/or failure to carry insurance on an uninterrupted basis are grounds for disciplinary action and grounds for denial of an application for licensure, denial of an application to renew a license, or suspension or revocation of a license. (See 193E Chapter 19.)
Individuals whose licenses are on inactive status with the IREC are not required to carry E&O insurance.

Iowa Real Estate Commission's Contracted Insurance Provider The IREC contracts with an insurance provider for a group policy that is made available to all licensees. The coverage contains a provision prohibiting the provider from canceling a licensee's coverage. The law allows licensees the option to obtain independent coverage as long as the coverage meets the minimum standards adopted by the Commission. The
standards adopted by the Commission include minimum liability limits, permissible deductible limits, and the permissible exceptions to the E&O coverage. Licensees may not self-insure.

b.x: Many other professions and issues touch real estate brokerage. This unit discusses appraisal requirements, landlord-tenant activities, and forms of ownership recognized in Iowa.
Most real estate transactions require the services of appraisers and home inspectors. The licensing and certification requirements of these professions vary by state.

Although licensing is not required for appraising in Iowa, most appraisers in Iowa are licensed. Those who are licensed must meet federal requirements established in theUniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP). The enforcement agency is the Iowa Real Estate Appraiser Examining Board, located on the Web atwww.state.ia.us/government/com/prof/appraiser/home.html.

The various appraisal designations depend on experience. Initially, appraisers are called either associate residential or associate general appraisers. To upgrade to the next level of certified residential appraiser, an associate residential appraiser is required to log 2,500 hours (two years of experience). To upgrade from an associate general to a certified general appraiser requires 3,500 hours of experience in 30 months (of which half must be in nonresidential appraisals).
To obtain a copy of the current USPAP from the Appraisal Foundation's Web site, go to https://netforum.avectra.com/eWeb/DynamicPage.aspx?Site=TAF&WebCode=USPAP.
At present, there is no requirement for licensing home inspectors.
There are several forms of property ownership, but not all are recognized in Iowa. Some forms are only available to spouses, some are used in multifamily buildings, while others are used in business.

secs.h: Forms Of Ownership Recognized In Iowa

b.x: Iowa recognizes tenancy in common and joint tenancy. Life estates, created by will or by deed, are common in Iowa, too. Iowa does not recognize tenancy by the entirety.
Dower and Curtesy

Dower and curtesy are recognized in Iowa. In Iowa, a wife has an inchoate interest called dower in her husband's estate. Inchoate means a right not yet perfected. When the husband dies, the wife's inchoate dower interest becomes a right. Curtesy is the husband's inchoate interest in his wife's estate. By signing a deed with his wife, the husband signs away his inchoate curtesy interest. For example, a man owns an apartment building by himself and then marries. The husband sells the building, and the buyer's attorney demands that the husband's wife sign the deed. When asked why, the buyer's attorney remarks, "Because if the husband predeceases his wife, legally she would have a dower right to one-third of your acquired apartment building." By signing the deed, the wife relinquishes her inchoate and subsequent dower rights.
Separate and Community Property

In Iowa, married couples may be able to designate separate and community property. Property that has been so commingled that it cannot be separated is known as community property in Iowa. When community property is disputed, it is normally divided 50-50. Iowa Code

Chapter 596 establishes the Iowa Uniform Premarital Agreement Act, allowing the prospective spouses to contract for future rights and obligations and to agree to keep designated properties separate from community property. However, in divorce court, child support and custody obligations may influence the outcome of a premarital agreement.

Ownership By Corporations And Partnerships Real estate brokerages in Iowa may include sole proprietorships, partnerships, limited liability company (LLC) operations, corporations, and subchapter S corporations. The following chapters from the Code of Iowa provide more rules for these forms of ownership:

i: Chapter 486 and 486A, "Uniform Partnership Law"
Chapter 487, "Uniform Limited Partnership Law"
Chapter 490, "Business Corporations"
Chapter 490A, "Limited Liability Companies"

b.x: Time-shares are a form of ownership interest that includes the use of a property for a fixed or variable period. A filing fee must accompany each initial filing, and consolidating additional time-shares requires an additional fee. Fees are paid through the Iowa Real Estate Commission (IREC).

The Iowa Time-Share Act covers rules for time-shares. The Act is divided into two parts. Sections 557A.4—557A.10 apply only to time-share programs located in Iowa, while Sections 557A.1, 557A.2, and 557A.11-20 apply to any time-share program, wherever located, that is marketed in Iowa.
Time-Shares and Real Estate Licensing

Any person engaged in the business or occupation of selling time-share estates for a fee or a commission is required to obtain a real estate license. Without a license, a person may only sell time-share uses, which are merely the right to use a property for a given period each year because no fee ownership is transferred.
Time-Share Purchaser's Rights

Under certain circumstances, time-share purchasers may rescind their contract. There is a cooling-off period. A purchaser may at any time within five business days following the receipt of all required information rescind in writing the contract of sale without stating any reason and without liability on the purchaser's part. All payments made before the decision to rescind must be refunded within 30 days after receipt of the notice to rescind.

Cooperatives and condominiums are examples of multiple owners of the same property. Articles of incorporation, bylaws, definitions, and restrictive covenants are all different; therefore, due diligence is required before making a decision to purchase. The condo buyer receives a deed to real property. The co-op buyer receives personal property in the form of shares of stock inseparable from the proprietary lease. The licensee who assists buyers in buying either type of property should always insist that the buyer read all relevant documents before entering into a purchase agreement.

There are different forms of condo ownership. Purchasers can own the interior surfaces of the unit, while the homeowners' association owns the exterior and the grounds. In this situation, the residential homeowner would need to purchase a condominium homeowners' insurance policy
(HO-6). The HO-6 covers interior surfaces such as cabinets, paint, floor coverings, and wall coverings.

In Iowa, some condominium associations own both the interior surfaces and the exteriors. In those cases, the residential purchaser buys renters' insurance (HO-4), and the tenant is prohibited (without written permission) from painting, recarpeting, or remodeling.

In other cases, such as with condominium town houses, the owner can own both the interior surfaces and the exterior. In this case the owner would need a regular homeowners' insurance policy (HO-2 or HO-3).
Iowa Laws that Govern Cooperatives and Condominium Ownership

In a cooperative, the association or corporation owns the property. Iowa Code Chapter 499A, "Multiple Housing," governs cooperative housing. By purchasing shares in the cooperative, the purchaser becomes an owner-tenant. The real estate is taxed in the name of the cooperative, but the individual owner-tenants are allowed to take tax deductions for the individual amounts paid as well as the same homestead tax credit and exemption as those afforded individual property owners.

In condominium ownership, the individual dwelling owner is individually taxed. Iowa Code Chapter 499B, "Horizontal Property," covers condominium housing. It is important to remember that condominium is a form of ownership, not a style of building. Condo ownership is not limited to residential units; office buildings, boat slips, and parking spaces can be owned as condominiums, too.
Unpaid Association Dues

All association dues assessed by the council of co-owners for the share of the common expenses chargeable to any unit creates a lien. If unpaid, the unit can be foreclosed on by suit from the council of co-owners or the association management company representing the co-owners. As a result, nonpayment of association dues as a form of protest is not an option.

The rules governing the relationship between the property owner (or a designated property manager) and the tenant have evolved over the years. Tenants' rights have increased and landlords must take care to avoid violating these rights or face financial penalties.

Laws Governing Landlord And Tenant Relations Landlord-tenant relations are covered in Iowa law. Chapter 562A of the Iowa Code is titled "Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Law." Chapter 562A is designed to simplify, clarify, modernize, and revise the laws governing the rental of dwelling units and the rights and obligations of both landlords and tenants, and to encourage them to maintain and improve the quality of housing. In addition, the law ensures that the right to the receipt of rent is inseparable from the duty to maintain the premises.

Anyone who manages even one unit should have a copy of this law and consult it frequently. The practice in years past of the landlord or the manager simply changing the locks and tossing the tenant's belongings into the street is no longer appropriate. Today, the tenant has enforceable rights, and the landlord who violates these rights may be faced with financial penalties.

To receive legal recognition in the judicial system, Iowa Code, Section 622.32, "Statute of Frauds," requires that all lease agreements for more than one year be in writing. While an oral lease for less than a year is enforceable, it is always best to get any lease in writing.

The requirements for holding a security deposit are defined in Iowa Code, Section 562A.12. This law prohibits a landlord from collecting security deposits in excess of the value of two months' rent. These funds must be deposited in a financial institution that is FDIC-insured or NCUA-insured. Rental deposits are to be placed in a trust account and are not to be commingled with the landlord's personal funds. Landowners can use interest-bearing common trust accounts for rental security deposits and collect (for the first five years) the earned interest income.

All eligible deposits must be returned to the vacated tenants within 30 days of termination. Bad-faith retention is subject to a fine and payment of reasonable attorney fees. In some circumstances, the penalty can be as much as three times the funds wrongfully withheld.

A landlord must follow specific procedures to evict a tenant. Legal notice has to be given, and a judge decides whether the eviction action is appropriate. Legally, after a landlord serves a material noncompliance notice, a tenant can be evicted in seven days unless the tenant comes into compliance. If the same problem, after compliance, recurs within six months, the rental agreement can be terminated in seven days.

If rent (when due and payable) is unpaid, and the tenant fails to pay the rent within three days after a written notice is served that also states that the landlord intends to evict the tenant, the rental agreement may be terminated. Where a lessee holds over after the termination of a lease
and proper service has been completed, Iowa Code Chapter 648, titled "Forcible Entry" or "Detention," provides judicial action through the district court.

b.x: A property's title marketability and transferability as well as its value can be affected by encumbrances. This unit covers basic information about Iowa-specific rules regarding encumbrances such as licenses, easements, property taxes, and adverse possession. Also covered is zoning regulations, which also affect the property's title.
A house payment is usually called PITI, which means principal, interest, taxes, and insurance. Real estate taxes may be a significant portion of the owner's monthly house payment, and a big
factor in the buying decision process. Because of this, agents should understand basic principles regarding property tax computations.
Property Assessment

Property tax is sometimes called an ad valorem tax, meaning based on the value or according to the value of the property. In theory, this is a fair way to raise revenue because landowners pay in proportion to the value of their property. The assessor uses an appraising method known as the sales comparison approach when computing market value. In other words, the assessor compares the selling prices of similar properties to determine market value of properties that have not sold recently.

In Iowa, the assessor's office uses the same appraising principles as appraisers. The assessor's selected properties (comparables) must meet certain criteria. First, a reasonable amount of time must be allowed for exposure to the open market. Also, the assessor may not use as comparables those properties sold to related parties or sold under undue influence, such as divorce, bankruptcy, adjoining land sales, zoning changes, and so forth. Both parties to the sale must have been well informed about the property and are assumed to have acted prudently and knowledgeably. Payment for the property must be made in cash or its equivalent, and financing must not have any negative effect on the property's true value.

As a helpful tool, the recorder's office and the assessor's office require the use of a Declaration of Value for every real estate transfer in Iowa. This form mandates the reporting of the actual purchase price, the financial details of any contract-for-deed sales, and from a long checklist, all relating sales conditions to the transfer. By using this form, the assessor is better apt to use valid comparables when trying to determine a property's assessed value.

After a property has been reassessed, the assessor's office notifies the taxpayer in early April of any changes. Taxpayers are allowed to protest their proposed assessmentbetween April 16 and May 5. Once the board of review reaches a decision on a taxpayer's appeal, a written notice is forwarded, and the assessor notifies the auditor's office, usually before the end of May, of the final jurisdictional property value.
Assessment Ratio (Rollback)

Once the jurisdictional property value has been determined, the auditor's office applies a state-mandated assessment ratio (rollback) to determine the property's taxable value. The Department of Revenue is the state agency that determines the rollback percentage for residential, commercial, agricultural, industrial, utilities, and exempt properties in Iowa. After applying the rollback, the auditor determines the appropriate tax rate. (For clarification, Iowa's rollback system began in 1977 during an unprecedented inflationary spiral. To prevent accelerated assessments from burdening property owners, a growth limit was placed on assessments. This growth limit is called a rollback.) Visitwww.iowa.gov/tax/locgov/propequalroll.html for more information.
Tax Rates

Tax rates are reflective of all approved state, county, city, school, and special budgets. Tax rates also consider all sources of income. After deducting the anticipated ancillary revenue derived from government reimbursements, gasoline taxes, fines, sales taxes, motel/hotel taxes, and so forth, from the approved budgets, the remainder necessary to cover the costs of the approved budgets is divided by the appropriate taxable value to determine the tax rate. Iowa's fiscal year begins on July 1 of one calendar year and ends on June 30 of the next calendar year.

Obviously, the tax levy varies with each taxing district. The decimal equivalent may be converted into a percentage. For example, a 0.045 tax rate would convert to 4.5 percent of a property's taxable value.

In Iowa, if taxpayers claim the purchased property as their personal residence (residing in the property at least six months out of the year), they are allowed an annual homestead tax deduction from the taxable value of their residence. This annual deduction is only allowed on one property at a time. It must be filed by the taxpayer before July 1 in order for the auditor's office to accomplish its tax calculations before tax statements are mailed out on or about September 1. Visitwww.iowa.gov/tax/taxlaw/PropertyTaxCredits.html#Homestead.

In addition to a homestead tax exemption, the Iowa military exemption reduces the taxable value of property for military veterans. The amount of exemption varies. The veteran must own the property on July 1 of each claim year. A qualified veteran must file a claim with the local assessor by July 1; subsequent claims do not need to be filed on the same property. Visit www.iowa.gov/tax/taxlaw/PropertyTaxCredits.html#Military for more information.
Iowa's Homestead Exemption

In Iowa, the homestead of every person is exempt from judicial sale where there is no statutory declaration to the contrary. Homestead protects the homeowner from a forced sale by any unsecured lienholder. Secured lienholders, such as lenders and owners who sell on contract, require that purchasers waive their homestead rights as a prerequisite to the contract. Until the property owner decides to transfer ownership, the entire homestead is exempt. Homestead exemption requests must be filed before July 1.

Property tax statements are annually mailed out by the county treasurer's office on September 1. The taxpayer's September notice is for the entire previous fiscal year. Iowa's fiscal year begins on July 1 of one calendar year and ends on June 30 of the next calendar year. The taxpayer is allowed to pay the amount due in two installments. If this option is chosen, the first-half installment is due before September 30 and the second before March 31.

As noted, Iowa property taxes are paid in arrears. The September installment (first half) pays for the first half of the previous fiscal year (July–December), while the March installment (second half) pays for the second half of the previous fiscal year (January–June). Property tax statements are annually mailed to taxpayers on or about September 1.
For further information on the tax process, access "An Introduction to Iowa Property Tax" at www.iowa.gov/tax/educate/78573.html.

When the property owner sells, taxes are divided into current taxes (those due but not delinquent) and prorated taxes (those due but not payable). Normally, the selling taxpayer pays the taxes that are due but not delinquent and prorates those that are due but not payable to the buyer. In some situations, such as a farm sale, taxes owed by the seller can be quite high.

In Iowa, property taxes paid in installments require that the first installment be paid before September 30. The taxes are considered late October 1. The second-half installment is due before March 30 and considered late on April 1. The delinquency penalty is 1.5 percent per month or 18 percent annually. If taxes are delinquent after one year, the property may be sold at a tax sale.

In Iowa, property owners are allowed one year from the date of delinquency to make restitution and pay the appropriate penalty before the delinquent property is placed up for tax sale. The tax sale in Iowa is the third Monday in June, and the tax sale funds are used to pay the delinquent property taxes. The purchaser at a tax sale is given a tax certificate, not a deed.

After a property is sold at a tax sale, the delinquent taxpayer has up to one year (the statutory right of redemption period in Iowa) to repurchase the property from the purchaser. Within one year, the delinquent taxpayer may pay the delinquent taxes plus interest, court, and advertising costs to regain the property. The person who paid the taxes (who bought at the tax sale) is entitled to an 18 percent return on the investment. If the delinquent taxpayer fails to repurchase the property within the statutory period, a tax deed is conveyed to the purchaser, and time runs out for the delinquent taxpayer to reclaim the tax-sale property.
An encumbrance is anything that diminishes the value or impairs the use or enjoyment of a property. The rules for certain types of encumbrances, such as easements and mechanics' liens, vary by state.

A mechanic's lien is a statutory lien created in favor of contractors, laborers, and suppliers who have performed work or furnished materials in the erection or repair of a building. The mechanic's lien is an equitable lien.

In Iowa, to initiate a mechanic's lien, the contractor or subcontractor files a lien with the clerk of the district court in the county where the material or labor was furnished or conducted. The lien
must be filed within 90 days of completion of the work. On filing, a copy of the lien is forwarded to the owner, the agent, or the trustee.

In Iowa, mechanics' liens have priority over each other based on the date and time filed. It is possible for a mechanic's lien to be filed after closing if the work has been performed within the stipulated time frame. It is effective as to the time that the work was performed. It might be noted that no notice must be given to the owner before filing a mechanic's lien.
Easements in Iowa can be created by deed or by use. If by deed, the Iowa Supreme Court requires that deed completion be done by a licensed attorney.

A prescriptive easement is created by using someone else's property openly (visibly), notoriously, and without permission for a statutory period of ten years. Should a landowner sell a landlocked parcel of real estate, implied consent is given for an easement. This is called an easement by necessity. Easements can be created by mutual agreement, and maintenance easements can be used in homeowners' association agreements.

Another term that is used when someone is given permission to use another's property is license. The word license has different meanings. In real estate usage, it can mean permission. For example, landowners can allow a party to go hunting or fishing on their property or to enter the property to pick apples or get water from a spring. A license is personal privilege, and as such, it is considered revocable permission, not a right that transfers with ownership.
Easements may be created by adverse possession. This occurs by someone's open, notorious, hostile and continuous possession of the property. In all actions in which title to any

ownership in real estate is claimed by virtue of adverse possession, the legally evidenced time frame in Iowa is ten years. To prevent an adverse possession claim, when any person is engaged in the use of a way, privilege, or other easement in the land of another, the owner of the land in question should serve written notice of intent to dispute any right arising from such claim or use.

Zoning is the regulation of structures and uses of property within designated areas or zones. Development of land through subdividing and construction is intended to put the land to its most profitable use. Regulation of all these activities is performed at the local level of government and impacts a property's title.

Iowa communities must have the legal authority to enforce zoning. Iowa Code Chapter 414, "City Zoning," grants cities the authority to regulate and restrict development in order to promote the health, safety, morals, or general welfare of the community. To avail itself of the powers conferred by Iowa law, each city of this state must appoint a zoning commission that sets forth the community's development goals and objectives (comprehensive plan). Zoning officials also create a board of adjustments to handle complaints and petitions for variance.

Special zoning for planned unit developments (PUDs) is utilized in Iowa to allow for diverse land uses (residential, commercial, and recreational) to exist under one umbrella. Converted-use properties need zoning approval (e.g., when warehouses in downtown areas are converted to loft apartments).

To ensure harmonious growth in conformity with community standards, land developers must adhere to the municipality's subdivision and land development regulations. The land must be surveyed and laid out so that the subdivision utilizes natural drainage and land contours. Often an environmental impact report is required along with the application for subdivision approval. Plats have to be adopted by the municipality before they can be recorded.

From the subdivision plans, plats are drawn of the land. The plat divides the land into lots. The plat is then submitted to the municipality for adoption. Often the developer pays the costs for the streets and sewers, and the streets and sewers are then dedicated back to the municipality for its ownership and their future maintenance.

Iowa is a home-rule state, which means that while building officials and builders agree to build according to the International Residential Code (IRC) standards, local building officials and builders (when applicable) can deviate somewhat and adopt alternative standards allowed under the Uniform Building Code (UBC).

Members of the National Association of Homebuilders build according to the IRC, which replaces the UBC. In addition, the International Building Code is the standard used for commercial building practices in the United States. All builders utilize standards established by the International Plumbing Code as well as the energy code known as CABO.
